modules.title: Hello, C
modules.summary: Your first programs. What main() is, how printf prints text, and how to read the compiler's complaints.

steps.title: Your first program
hints: The function that prints text is spelled `printf` (print formatted).

steps.title: Printing your own text
steps.text:
Whatever is between the double quotes is printed exactly. The quotes themselves are not printed.

Note the `;` at the end of the statement. In C, statements end with a semicolon, like a period ends a sentence.

**Your turn:** make the program print exactly:

```
I am learning C
```
hints: Type the sentence between the quotes. Capital letters and spaces matter.

steps.title: Several lines
steps.text:
Each `printf` call continues where the last one stopped. Only `\n` moves to a new line, so these two calls:

```c
printf("Ready, ");
printf("set\n");
```

print `Ready, set` on a single line.

**Your turn:** write a program that prints these three lines:

```
Counter-Strike
is a game
about aim
```
hints: Add one `printf` per line. Each one needs `\n` at the end of the text.
The second line is `printf("is a game\n");`

tests.name: Output
tests.expect:
Counter-Strike
is a game
about aim

steps.title: Escape sequences
steps.text:
Some characters can't be typed directly inside a string, so C uses **escape sequences** that start with a backslash:

| You write | You get |
|---|---|
| `\n` | new line |
| `\t` | tab |
| `\"` | a double quote |
| `\\` | a backslash |

**Your turn:** print this line exactly, including the quotes:

```
She said "gg" and left
```
hints: A plain `"` would end the string early. Write `\"` for each quote you want printed.

steps.title: Comments and reading errors
steps.text:
Comments are notes for humans. The compiler ignores them.

```c
// a comment runs to the end of the line
/* this kind can span
   several lines */
```

When the code is wrong, the compiler tells you the **line number** and what it expected. The most common beginner error is a missing semicolon: `error: expected ';'`.

**Your turn:** this program has two mistakes. Press **Check** first to see what the compiler says, then fix both so it prints `Fixed it` on one line.
hints: The compiler points at the line where it noticed the problem, which is sometimes the line *after* the real mistake.
Both `printf(...)` and `return 0` need a `;` at the end.

modules.title: Variables and types
modules.summary: Store values in named boxes. int, double and char, printing them with format specifiers, and constants.

steps.title: Your first variable
steps.text:
A **variable** is a named box that holds a value. In C you must say what *type* of value goes in the box.

```c
int kills = 25;
```

This creates a box named `kills` that holds an `int` (a whole number) and puts `25` in it.

To print it, `printf` needs a **format specifier** where the value should go. For an `int` that's `%d`:

```c
printf("Kills: %d\n", kills);
```

**Your turn:** declare an `int` named `score` with the value `42`.
hints: The type for whole numbers is `int`.

steps.title: Printing values with %d
steps.text:
`printf` replaces each `%d` with the next value after the format string, in order.

```c
int a = 3, b = 4;
printf("%d + %d\n", a, b);   // prints 3 + 4
```

**Your turn:** complete the `printf` so it prints `K/D: 20/5`.
hints: Put a `%d` for each number, then list the variables after the string in the same order.

steps.title: Changing a variable
steps.text:
A variable can be given a new value with `=`. The old value is replaced.

```c
int hp = 100;
hp = hp - 27;     // now 73
```

Read `hp = hp - 27` as: take the current value of `hp`, subtract 27, and store the result back in `hp`.

**Your turn:** the player has `3200` money and buys a rifle for `2700`. Subtract the price from `money` so the program prints `Money left: 500`.
hints: Write `money = money - 2700;` on the empty line.

require.message: Change `money` itself by subtracting 2700 from it (don't just print 500).

steps.title: Decimals with double
steps.text:
`int` can't hold fractions. For numbers with a decimal point use `double`, and print it with `%f`.

```c
double accuracy = 0.625;
printf("%f\n", accuracy);    // 0.625000
printf("%.2f\n", accuracy);  // 0.63 (rounded to 2 places)
```

`%.2f` means "two digits after the decimal point".

**Your turn:** store `1.25` in a `double` named `rating` and print it with exactly two decimals so the output is `Rating: 1.25`.
hints: The type is `double`. The format for two decimals is `%.2f`.

steps.title: Characters with char
steps.text:
A `char` holds a single character, written in **single** quotes: `'A'`. Double quotes make a string, which is a different thing.

Print a `char` with `%c`:

```c
char grade = 'B';
printf("Grade: %c\n", grade);
```

Under the hood a `char` is a small number (its ASCII code), so `'A'` is 65. Printing a char with `%d` shows that number.

**Your turn:** write a program that stores the letter `T` in a `char` named `team`, then prints two lines:

```
Team: T
Code: 84
```
hints: `char team = 'T';` declares it.
Use `%c` for the letter and `%d` for its number code.

require.message: Declare a variable named `team` of type `char`.

steps.title: Constants and sizeof
steps.text:
Put `const` in front of a declaration to make a variable read-only. Trying to change it later is a compile error, which protects you from accidents.

```c
const int MAX_PLAYERS = 10;
```

`sizeof` tells you how many bytes a type uses. On this site (and most machines) `int` is 4 bytes, `double` is 8 and `char` is always 1. Print a size with `%zu`.

**Your turn:** declare a constant `int` named `ROUND_TIME` equal to `115`, and print:

```
Round time: 115
int bytes: 4
```
hints: The keyword that makes a variable read-only is `const`.
`sizeof(int)` gives the size of an int in bytes.

modules.title: Operators and math
modules.summary: Arithmetic, the integer-division trap, the % remainder operator, precedence, shorthand operators and casts.

steps.title: Arithmetic
steps.text:
C has the usual math operators: `+`, `-`, `*` (multiply) and `/` (divide).

```c
int total = 12 * 3 + 4;   // 40
```

Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, just like in school math. Parentheses change the order: `12 * (3 + 4)` is 84.

**Your turn:** make the program print `Damage: 96` by filling in the operators. Base damage is 30, the multiplier is 4, armor absorbs 24.
hints: 30 times 4 is 120, and 120 minus 24 is 96.

steps.title: The integer division trap
steps.text:
When **both** sides of `/` are `int`, C does integer division: the fraction is thrown away (not rounded).

```c
printf("%d\n", 7 / 2);      // 3, not 3.5
printf("%f\n", 7.0 / 2);    // 3.500000
```

If either side is a `double`, you get a real division.

**Your turn:** 25 kills over 10 rounds should print `Kills per round: 2.50`. Right now it prints `2.00`. Fix the calculation of `kpr` so it does a real division.
hints: `kills / rounds` is computed as int / int (giving 2) *before* it's stored in the double.
Turn one side into a double first. Write `(double)kills / rounds`. That `(double)` is called a *cast*.

steps.title: Remainder with %
steps.text:
`%` (modulo) gives the **remainder** of an integer division.

```c
17 / 5   // 3
17 % 5   // 2   (17 = 3*5 + 2)
```

It's great for "is this even?" (`n % 2 == 0`) and for splitting units.

**Your turn:** a match lasted `754` seconds. Print it as minutes and seconds: `12 min 34 sec`.
hints: Minutes are how many whole 60s fit into total, so `total / 60`.
Seconds are what's left over, so `total % 60`.

require.message: Use the `%` operator on `total` to get the seconds.

steps.title: Shorthand operators
steps.text:
Updating a variable with itself is so common that C has shortcuts:

| Shorthand | Means |
|---|---|
| `x += 5;` | `x = x + 5;` |
| `x -= 5;` | `x = x - 5;` |
| `x *= 2;` | `x = x * 2;` |
| `x++;` | `x = x + 1;` |
| `x--;` | `x = x - 1;` |

**Your turn:** fill in the shorthand operators so the program prints `Streak: 12`.
hints: The comments say what each line should do: add 1, double, add 1, subtract 1.

steps.title: Prefix vs postfix ++
steps.text:
`x++` and `++x` both add 1 to `x`, but they differ when used inside a bigger expression:

- `x++` (postfix) gives the **old** value, then increments.
- `++x` (prefix) increments first, then gives the **new** value.

```c
int a = 5;
int b = a++;   // b = 5, a = 6
int c = ++a;   // a = 7, c = 7
```

**Your turn:** make the program print `5 7 7` by choosing prefix or postfix for each blank. The variable `a` starts at 5.
hints: `b` must get the old value 5, so use postfix: `a++`. After that, `a` is 6.
`c` must be 7 and `a` must also be 7, so increment first: `++a`.

steps.title: Put it together
steps.text:
Time to write a small calculation on your own.

A player's **ADR** (average damage per round) is total damage divided by rounds played. Given the variables below, print:

```
Total damage: 2090
ADR: 83.60
```

Total damage is the sum of the three halves' damage (it's a long match: first half, second half, overtime).
hints: Add the three variables into an `int total`.
Watch out for integer division: `(double)total / rounds`.
Print with `%d` for the total and `%.2f` for the ADR.

forbid.message: Compute the numbers from the variables instead of typing the answers.

modules.title: Reading input
modules.summary: Make programs interactive with scanf. Reading numbers, characters and words, and checking that the read worked.

steps.title: Read a number
steps.text:
`scanf` is the mirror image of `printf`: it reads values from input (stdin) into variables.

```c
int n;
scanf("%d", &n);
```

The `&` means "the address of `n`". scanf needs to know *where* to store the value, not what's currently in it. Forgetting `&` is the #1 scanf bug.

On this site, each test feeds the program some input. Use **Run with my input** to try your own.

**Your turn:** read an int and print it doubled. Input `21` prints `42`.
hints: scanf needs the address of the variable, written `&n`.

steps.title: Several values at once
steps.text:
One `scanf` can read several values. Whitespace (spaces, newlines) between them is skipped automatically for numbers.

```c
int a, b;
scanf("%d %d", &a, &b);
```

**Your turn:** read a player's kills and deaths and print their difference.

Input: `18 11` prints `+/-: 7`
hints: `scanf("%d %d", &kills, &deaths);`

steps.title: Reading doubles
hints: Read with `scanf("%lf", &c);`
Compute `double f = c * 9 / 5 + 32;` then print with `%.1f`.

steps.title: Characters and words
steps.text:
- `%c` reads **one character**, and it does *not* skip whitespace. Write `" %c"` (with a leading space) to skip spaces and newlines first.
- `%s` reads a **word** (up to the next space) into a char array. Arrays don't need `&`. You'll learn why in the pointers module.

```c
char name[32];
scanf("%31s", name);   // 31 = max chars, leaving room for the terminator
```

**Your turn:** the input is a name followed by a team letter, like `s1mple T`. Print `s1mple plays on T`.
hints: The format for one char is `%c`. The space before it in the format string skips the space in the input.
team is a plain char variable, so scanf needs its address, `&team`.

steps.title: Did the read work?
hints: Replace the `0` with the scanf call and compare its result: `scanf("%d", &n) == 1`.

modules.title: Making decisions
modules.summary: if, else if and else. Comparison and logical operators, switch, and the ternary operator.

steps.title: if and else
hints: The structure is `if (condition) { ... } else { ... }`.
The condition is "hp greater than 0", written `hp > 0`.

steps.title: else if chains
hints: Start with the biggest case (`k >= 5`) so smaller checks don't catch it first.
Order: `>= 5`, then `>= 2`, then `== 1`, then `else`.

steps.title: And, or, not
steps.text:
Combine conditions with logical operators:

- `&&` (and): true only if **both** sides are true
- `||` (or): true if **at least one** side is true
- `!` (not): flips true and false

```c
if (money >= 2700 && !has_rifle) { ... }
```

In C, any non-zero number counts as true and `0` is false.

**Your turn:** read `money` and `round` (two ints). A player can buy if they have at least 2700 money **and** it is not the first round (round 1 is a pistol round). Print `buy` or `save`.
hints: Two conditions joined by `&&`: `money >= 2700` and `round != 1`.

steps.title: switch
hints: Keywords used here: `switch`, `break`, `case`, `default`.
Without the `break` after forward, pressing w would also print left.

steps.title: The ternary operator
hints: The pattern is `condition ? value_if_true : value_if_false`.

steps.title: Challenge: leap years
steps.text:
A year is a leap year if:

- it's divisible by 4, **and**
- it's **not** divisible by 100, **unless** it's also divisible by 400.

So 2024 and 2000 are leap years, but 1900 and 2023 are not.

**Your turn:** read a year and print `leap` or `common`.
hints: "Divisible by 4" is `y % 4 == 0`.
Leap if (divisible by 4 and not by 100) or divisible by 400.

modules.title: Loops
modules.summary: Repeat work with while, for and do-while. break, continue, nested loops and loop-driven input.

steps.title: while loops
hints: Keep looping while n is at least 1, and decrease n each time.
The update is `n--`.

steps.title: for loops
hints: Loop `i` from 1 up to and including n, so the condition is `i <= n`.
Inside, print `i * i` followed by a space. (Trailing spaces at the end of a line are ignored by the checker.)

require.message: Use a `for` loop.

steps.title: Accumulating a total
steps.text:
A very common loop pattern: start a variable at 0 and add to it every round.

```c
int sum = 0;
for (int i = 1; i <= 100; i++) {
    sum += i;
}
```

**Your turn:** the first number of input is `n`, followed by `n` damage values. Print the total damage and the highest single hit:

Input:
```
4
27 100 64 9
```
Output:
```
total 200
max 100
```
hints: Loop n times. Each round, read one value with scanf.
Add each value to total. If it's bigger than max, update max.

steps.title: break and continue
hints: `if (x == 0) break;`
`if (x < 0) continue;` then `sum += x;`

require.message: Use `break` to stop at 0.
Use `continue` to skip negative numbers.

steps.title: do-while
hints: Structure: `do { read; if invalid, print; } while (invalid);`
Invalid means `x < 1 || x > 5`.

require.message: Use a `do { ... } while (...);` loop.

steps.title: Nested loops
hints: Row number `row` (starting at 1) has exactly `row` hashes.
The inner loop runs `row` times and prints `#`. After it, print a newline.

modules.title: Functions
modules.summary: Split programs into named, reusable pieces. Parameters, return values, prototypes, scope and recursion.

steps.title: Define and call a function
hints: The function returns an int, so the return type is `int`.
`return` sends a value back to the caller.

steps.title: Write a function
steps.text: **Your turn:** write `int max3(int a, int b, int c)` that returns the largest of three numbers.

hints: Keep a running best. Start with `int m = a;` and compare it with b, then c.

steps.title: void functions
hints: Loop n times printing `=`, then print `\n` once after the loop.

steps.title: Prototypes
hints: A prototype is the first line of the function with a semicolon: `int half(int x);`
Put it after the `#include` and before `main`.

require.message: Add a prototype `int half(int x);` above main (keep the definition below).

steps.title: Scope and pass by value
steps.text:
Variables declared inside a function only exist inside it (**local scope**).

C passes arguments **by value**: the function gets a *copy*. Changing the parameter doesn't change the caller's variable:

```c
void reset(int hp) { hp = 100; }   // changes the copy only

int hp = 20;
reset(hp);
printf("%d\n", hp);   // still 20
```

(To change the caller's variable you need pointers, coming soon.)

**Your turn:** `heal` below tries to modify its parameter. Rewrite it to **return** the new value instead, and store that result in `main` so the program prints `hp 75`.
hints: Change the return type to `int` and `return hp + amount;`.
In main, store the result: `hp = heal(hp, 25);`

forbid.message: Let heal() compute the value.

steps.title: Recursion
steps.text:
A function can call itself. That's **recursion**. Every recursive function needs a **base case** that stops, and a step that moves toward it.

```c
int factorial(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return 1;          // base case
    return n * factorial(n - 1);   // smaller problem
}
```

**Your turn:** write `int fib(int n)` returning the n-th Fibonacci number, where `fib(0) = 0`, `fib(1) = 1` and every later number is the sum of the two before it.
steps.seed:

}
hints: Base cases: if n is 0 or 1, return n.
Otherwise return `fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)`.

steps.title: Challenge: is it prime?
steps.text:
A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself.

**Your turn:** write `int is_prime(int n)` that returns `1` for primes and `0` otherwise. Only test divisors up to the square root (`d * d <= n`) so it stays fast for big numbers.

hints: Anything below 2 is not prime.
Try every d from 2 while `d * d <= n`. If `n % d == 0`, it's not prime.

modules.title: Arrays
modules.summary: Store many values of one type side by side. Indexing, looping, passing arrays to functions and 2D grids.

steps.title: Declare and index
steps.text:
An **array** is a fixed-size row of values of the same type, stored next to each other in memory.

```c
int ammo[3] = {30, 20, 7};
printf("%d\n", ammo[0]);   // 30, indexes start at 0
ammo[2] = 8;               // change the last one
```

An array of size 3 has valid indexes **0, 1, 2**. `ammo[3]` is out of bounds. C won't stop you, and the result is undefined behaviour.

**Your turn:** print the first and the last element of the array.
hints: The first index is 0. With 5 elements, the last index is 4.

steps.title: Loop over an array
hints: Sum the elements in a for loop from 0 to n - 1.
Divide as doubles: `(double)sum / n`, then print with `%.2f`.

forbid.message: Compute the average with a loop instead of hard-coding it.

You can `scanf` directly into an element: `scanf("%d", &a[i]);`

**Your turn:** input is `n` (at most 100) followed by `n` numbers. Print them in **reverse** order on one line, separated by spaces.

Input `4` / `1 2 3 4` prints `4 3 2 1`.
hints: First loop reads with `scanf("%d", &a[i]);`
Second loop counts down: `for (int i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)`.

modules.title: Strings
modules.summary: C strings are char arrays ending in '\0'. Length, copying, comparing, and writing string functions yourself.

steps.title: The null terminator
steps.text:
C has no built-in string type. A string is a **char array** that ends with the special character `'\0'` (value 0), called the **null terminator**.

```c
char name[] = "dust";
// stored as: 'd' 'u' 's' 't' '\0'   (5 chars!)
```

Functions like `printf("%s")` print characters until they hit `'\0'`. Forget it, and they keep reading random memory.

**Your turn:** build the string `"ak"` by hand and print it.
hints: The terminator character is written `'\0'` (backslash zero, in single quotes).

steps.title: strlen and friends
steps.text:
`<string.h>` has the standard string functions:

| Function | Does |
|---|---|
| `strlen(s)` | number of chars before `'\0'` |
| `strcpy(dst, src)` | copy src into dst |
| `strcat(dst, src)` | append src to dst |
| `strcmp(a, b)` | 0 if equal, negative/positive otherwise |

`dst` must be big enough, including room for the `'\0'`.

**Your turn:** read two words and print them joined with a `-` between, followed by the total length. Input `de dust2` prints `de-dust2 8`.
hints: Copy the first word in with `strcpy(out, a);`
Then `strcat(out, "-");` and `strcat(out, b);`

steps.title: Write your own strlen
steps.text:
Knowing how the library works makes you dangerous (in a good way). A string's length is the number of chars before `'\0'`.

**Your turn:** write `int my_strlen(const char s[])` without using `<string.h>`.

`const` here promises the function won't modify the string.

hints: Start a counter at 0 and move forward while `s[n] != '\0'`.

steps.title: Compare strings correctly
steps.text:
`a == b` on two strings compares their **addresses**, not their contents. To compare text, use `strcmp`:

```c
if (strcmp(map, "mirage") == 0) { ... }   // equal
```

**Your turn:** read a command word. Print `planting` for `plant`, `defusing` for `defuse`, and `unknown command` for anything else.
hints: `strcmp(cmd, "plant") == 0` is true when they match.

require.message: Compare the text with `strcmp`.

steps.title: Characters are numbers
steps.text:
Because chars are small numbers, you can do math on them. Letters `'a'` to `'z'` are consecutive, so `'a' + 2` is `'c'`, and `c - 'a'` gives a letter's position in the alphabet.

`<ctype.h>` has helpers: `isdigit(c)`, `isalpha(c)`, `isupper(c)`, `toupper(c)`, `tolower(c)`.

**Your turn:** write `void to_upper(char s[])` that converts every lowercase letter in the string to uppercase **in place**. Leave other characters alone.

hints: Loop until you reach `'\0'`.

steps.title: Challenge: palindromes
steps.text:
A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards, like `level` or `racecar`.

**Your turn:** write `int is_palindrome(const char s[])` returning 1 or 0. Compare characters from both ends moving inward, like reversing an array.
hints: Two indexes: `i = 0` and `j = strlen(s) - 1`.
While `i < j`, if `s[i] != s[j]` it's not a palindrome. Otherwise move both inward.

modules.title: Pointers
modules.summary: Addresses and the variables that hold them. & and *, changing a caller's variables, pointer arithmetic, arrays vs pointers, NULL and const.

steps.title: Addresses and pointers
steps.text:
Every variable lives at an **address** in memory. `&x` gives you that address. A **pointer** is a variable that stores an address.

```c
int hp = 100;
int *p = &hp;     // p points at hp
printf("%d\n", *p);   // 100: *p means "the value p points at"
*p = 75;              // changes hp itself!
printf("%d\n", hp);   // 75
```

- `int *p` declares "p is a pointer to int".
- `&hp` is "address of hp".
- `*p` (the **dereference** operator) is "the thing at that address".

**Your turn:** make `p` point at `armor`, then use `p` (not `armor` directly) to set it to `50`.
hints: The address of armor is `&armor`.
To write to the variable p points at, use `*p = ...`.

steps.title: Change the caller's variable
steps.seed:
void swap(int *a, int *b) {

}
hints: Save the value at a: `int tmp = *a;`
Then `*a = *b;` and `*b = tmp;`

steps.title: Returning two results
steps.text:
A function can only `return` one value. Pointer parameters let it hand back more ("out parameters"):

```c
void minmax(int a[], int n, int *min, int *max);
```

**Your turn:** write `void divmod(int a, int b, int *q, int *r)` that stores `a / b` in `*q` and `a % b` in `*r`.

hints: Write through the pointers: `*q = a / b;` and `*r = a % b;`

steps.title: Pointer arithmetic and arrays
steps.text:
An array's name turns into a pointer to its first element when you use it ("decays"). Adding 1 to a pointer moves it to the **next element** (not the next byte):

```c
int a[3] = {10, 20, 30};
int *p = a;          // same as &a[0]
printf("%d\n", *(p + 1));   // 20
```

In fact `a[i]` is defined as `*(a + i)`. That's why arrays passed to functions can be modified: the function receives a pointer to the original elements.

**Your turn:** write `int sum(const int *p, int n)` using pointer arithmetic instead of `[]`.

int sum(const int *p, int n) {

}
hints: `*(p + i)` is element i. Or walk the pointer itself: `s += *p; p++;`
One neat version: `for (const int *end = p + n; p < end; p++) s += *p;`

forbid.message: Use pointer arithmetic (`*p`, `p++`, `*(p + i)`) instead of `[ ]` on this step.

hints: Check `if (p == NULL) return fallback;` before touching `*p`.

steps.title: Strings through pointers
steps.seed:
int count_char(const char *s, char ch) {

}
hints: Walk the pointer until `*s == '\0'`, counting matches.

steps.title: Pointers to pointers
steps.seed:
void advance(const char **s) {

}
hints: `*s` is the caller's pointer, and `**s` is the character it points at.
While `**s == ' '`, move the caller's pointer: `(*s)++;` (parentheses matter).

steps.title: const and pointers
steps.text:
`const` can protect two different things, depending on where you put it:

| Declaration | Can change `*p`? | Can re-point `p`? |
|---|---|---|
| `const int *p` | no | yes |
| `int *const p` | yes | no |
| `const int *const p` | no | no |

Read it right to left: `const int *p` is "p is a pointer to an int that is const".

Professional C code marks every pointer parameter it only reads as `const int *`. It documents the promise ("I won't change your data") and the compiler enforces it.

A function can also **return** a pointer into the caller's array. If the array was `const`, the returned pointer must be `const` too.

**Your turn:** write `const int *find(const int *a, int n, int target)` that returns a pointer to the first element equal to `target`, or `NULL` if there is none.
hints: Loop over the n elements. When one equals target, return its address.
`return &a[i];` or, walking a pointer, `return p;`. After the loop, `return NULL;`.

steps.title: Two pointers from both ends
steps.seed:
void reverse(int *a, int n) {

}
hints: Start with `int *lo = a, *hi = a + n - 1;`.
While `lo < hi`: swap `*lo` and `*hi` with a temp, then `lo++; hi--;`.
Guard `n < 2` first, so you never compute `a - 1` for an empty array.

forbid.message: Use two pointers (`*lo`, `*hi`) instead of `[ ]` on this step.

steps.title: Challenge: squeeze out spaces
steps.text:
Another two-pointer classic: a **read** pointer scans every character, while a **write** pointer only advances when a character is kept. Everything happens in the same buffer, no extra memory.

```
"a b  c"      read ->  a _ b _ _ c
"abc"         write -> a b c \0
```

Don't forget to write the `'\0'` terminator at the final write position.

**Your turn:** write `void squeeze(char *s)` that removes every space from `s` in place.
steps.seed:
void squeeze(char *s) {

}
hints: Use two pointers into the same string: `char *w = s;` for writing and another for reading.
For every character that isn't a space, copy it with `*w = *r;` and move `w` forward.
After the loop, end the string: `*w = '\0';`

modules.title: Dynamic memory
modules.summary: The stack vs the heap. malloc, free, calloc and realloc, growing arrays, and who owns what.

steps.title: Stack vs heap
steps.text:
So far every variable lived on the **stack**: it's created when its block starts and destroyed automatically when the block ends. Stack arrays need a size known up front, and they die when the function returns.

The **heap** is memory you request at runtime and give back when you're done:

```c
#include <stdlib.h>

int *a = malloc(n * sizeof(int));   // room for n ints
if (a == NULL) { /* out of memory */ }
a[0] = 42;                          // use it like an array
free(a);                            // give it back
```

`malloc` returns `NULL` if it fails. Every `malloc` needs exactly one matching `free`.

**Your turn:** allocate room for `n` ints.
hints: `malloc(bytes)` allocates; the number of bytes is `n * sizeof(int)`.
The function that releases heap memory is `free`.

steps.title: Size decided at runtime
steps.text:
The real power of `malloc`: the size can come from input.

**Your turn:** read `n`, then `n` numbers into a heap array. Print how many are **above the average**. Free the array at the end.

Input `4` / `2 4 6 8` (average 5) prints `2`.
hints: `int *a = malloc(n * sizeof(int));`
Two passes. The first reads and sums, the second counts values greater than the average.
Compare with a double average: `a[i] > (double)sum / n`.

require.message: Allocate the array with `malloc` (the size comes from input).
Don't forget to `free` the array.

steps.title: Return heap memory from a function
hints: Allocate with malloc, fill it in a loop, and return the pointer.

steps.title: calloc and strdup-style copies
steps.text:
- `calloc(count, size)` allocates **and zeroes** the memory.
- To keep a copy of a string, allocate `strlen(s) + 1` bytes (the +1 is for `'\0'`) and copy it in.

**Your turn:** write `char *copy_string(const char *s)` that returns a new heap copy of `s`.
hints: Allocate `strlen(s) + 1` bytes.
Copy with `strcpy(c, s)` (or memcpy of n + 1 bytes) and return c.

steps.title: Growing with realloc
hints: Before storing, check `if (count == cap)`. If so, double cap and realloc.
`a[count++] = x;` stores and advances in one go.

require.message: Grow the array with `realloc`.

steps.title: Memory bugs to avoid
steps.text:
The classic heap mistakes, which C won't catch for you:

| Bug | What happens |
|---|---|
| **Leak** | forgetting `free`; memory is lost until the program exits |
| **Use after free** | using a pointer after `free`; it may point at reused memory |
| **Double free** | freeing twice; corrupts the allocator |
| **Out of bounds** | writing past the end; silently corrupts neighbours |

A good habit: set a pointer to `NULL` right after freeing it. `free(NULL)` is safe and does nothing.

**Your turn:** this function should build a message but it has two memory bugs (a missing `+ 1` for the terminator, and a leak of `tmp`). Fix both so it returns `"gg wp"` correctly.
hints: "gg wp" needs 2 + 1 + 2 = 5 chars **plus** the terminator. Add `+ 1` to the size of `out`.
`tmp` is only a scratch copy. Call `free(tmp);` before returning.

require.message: `tmp` is never freed. That's a leak.
The size for `out` has no room for the `'\0'` terminator. Add `+ 1`.

steps.title: A 2D grid on the heap
steps.text:
When a grid's size is only known at runtime, a common layout is an **array of row pointers**, each row its own allocation:

```
grid ──> [ row0 ] ──> [ 0 0 0 0 ]
         [ row1 ] ──> [ 0 0 0 0 ]
         [ row2 ] ──> [ 0 0 0 0 ]
```

```c
int **g = malloc(rows * sizeof *g);        // the row pointers
for (int r = 0; r < rows; r++)
    g[r] = calloc(cols, sizeof *g[r]);     // each row, zeroed
```

`sizeof *g` means "the size of whatever g points at". It stays correct even if you change the type later, which is why many style guides prefer it.

Freeing goes in reverse: every row first, then the array of pointers. If any allocation fails halfway, free what you already allocated and return `NULL`.

**Your turn:** write `make_grid` (all cells zero) and `free_grid`.
hints: First `int **g = malloc(rows * sizeof *g);`, then a loop with `g[r] = calloc(cols, sizeof *g[r]);`.
free_grid: `free(g[r])` for every row, then `free(g)`. Return early if g is NULL.

require.message: After freeing each row, free the array of row pointers too: `free(g);`

steps.title: Who owns what
steps.text:
C has no garbage collector, so every heap pointer needs an **owner**: the one piece of code responsible for freeing it. Professional C code writes this down in a comment next to each function:

```c
/* Returns a new array of new strings. The caller owns both:
   free each word, then the array, or call free_words(). */
char **split_words(const char *s, int *count);
```

A function that allocates something nested usually ships a matching "free" function, so callers can't get the order wrong.

**Your turn:** write `split_words`. It splits `s` on single spaces into separately allocated strings, stores how many in `*count`, and returns the array. Then write `free_words`. You can assume words are separated by exactly one space and `s` has no leading or trailing spaces. An empty string has 0 words (you may return `NULL` then).
hints: First count the words: one more than the number of spaces (unless the string is empty).
Allocate `n` pointers, then for each word allocate `len + 1` bytes, `memcpy` the letters and add `'\0'`.
`strchr(start, ' ')` finds the next space, or returns NULL for the last word.
free_words frees every word, then the array. `free(NULL)` is safe, so the empty case needs nothing special.

steps.title: Challenge: a string builder
steps.text:
Building a long string with repeated `strcat` into a fixed buffer is how buffer overflows happen. Real C code uses a **string builder**: a struct that owns a growing heap buffer.

```c
typedef struct {
    char *buf;   /* always '\0'-terminated once initialized */
    size_t len;  /* characters used, not counting '\0' */
    size_t cap;  /* bytes allocated */
} Builder;
```

**Your turn:** write the four functions:

- `sb_init(b)`: allocate a small starting buffer (say 8 bytes) holding `""`. Return 0 on success, -1 if allocation fails.
- `sb_append(b, s)`: append `s`, doubling `cap` as many times as needed. Return 0, or -1 if `realloc` fails (leave `b` unchanged then).
- `sb_str(b)`: return the current string.
- `sb_free(b)`: free the buffer and reset the fields.
hints: sb_init: set cap to 8, len to 0, `malloc` the buffer and put `'\0'` in it.
sb_append: you need `len + strlen(s) + 1` bytes. Double a local copy of cap until it's enough, then `realloc` into a temp pointer.
Copy with `memcpy(b->buf + b->len, s, add + 1)` so the terminator comes along, then add to len.

modules.title: Structs, enums and typedef
modules.summary: Group related data into your own types. Struct members, arrays of structs, pointers with ->, enums and typedef.

steps.title: Define a struct
hints: Types you define with members use the `struct` keyword.
Members are accessed with a dot: `w.name`, `w.damage`.

steps.title: Structs in functions
steps.text:
Structs can be passed to and returned from functions like any value (the whole struct is copied).

**Your turn:** write `double kd(struct Player p)` that returns kills divided by deaths as a double. If deaths is 0, return the kills.
hints: Guard `p.deaths == 0` first.
Cast to avoid integer division: `(double)p.kills / p.deaths`.

steps.title: Pointers to structs and ->
hints: `p->kills += kills;`
`if (died) p->deaths++;`

steps.title: Arrays of structs
steps.text:
An array of structs is like a table: one struct per row.

**Your turn:** the input is `n` followed by `n` lines of `name kills`. Print the name of the player with the most kills (the first one wins ties).

```
3
ropz 18
broky 25
rain 25
```
prints `MVP: broky`.
hints: Read each row with `scanf("%31s %d", team[i].name, &team[i].kills);` (no & for the char array).
Track the index of the best so far, and only replace it on a strictly greater kill count.

steps.title: enum
steps.text:
An `enum` gives names to a set of integer constants, which makes code self-explanatory:

```c
enum Side { T, CT };            // T = 0, CT = 1
enum Side s = CT;
```

Enums pair perfectly with `switch`.

**Your turn:** write `const char *weapon_name(enum Weapon w)` that returns `"rifle"`, `"pistol"`, `"knife"` for the three enum values and `"?"` otherwise.
hints: `switch (w) { case RIFLE: return "rifle"; ... }`
Return `"?"` after the switch for anything unmatched.

steps.title: typedef
hints: Build the result: `Vec2 r = {a.x + b.x, a.y + b.y};` and return it.

modules.title: Linked data structures
modules.summary: Put structs, pointers and malloc together. Build a linked list and a stack from scratch.

steps.title: A node that points to a node
hints: b's next should be the address of c, written `&c`.
The walk stops when p becomes `NULL`, and moves with `p = p->next`.

steps.title: Push to the front
steps.text:
Real lists allocate nodes on the heap. Adding at the front is the easiest operation: the new node points at the old head, and becomes the new head.

The function has to change the caller's head pointer, so it takes a **pointer to the head pointer**:

```c
void push_front(struct Node **head, int value);
```

**Your turn:** implement it.
hints: Allocate a node: `struct Node *n = malloc(sizeof *n);`
Set `n->value`, point `n->next` at the current head (`*head`), then make `*head = n`.

steps.title: Length and sum
steps.text:
**Your turn:** write two traversal functions:

- `int list_length(const struct Node *head)`
- `int list_sum(const struct Node *head)`
hints: Walk with `for (const struct Node *p = head; p != NULL; p = p->next)`.

steps.title: Free the whole list
hints: Loop while head is not NULL.
Save `head->next` in a variable before calling `free(head)`.

steps.title: Reverse a linked list
steps.text:
A famous interview question. Walk the list once and flip every `next` pointer to point backwards. You'll need three pointers: `prev`, `cur`, and `next`.

**Your turn:** write `struct Node *reverse(struct Node *head)` that returns the new head.
hints: Start with `prev = NULL`, `cur = head`.
Each step: save `next = cur->next`, set `cur->next = prev`, then move `prev = cur` and `cur = next`.
When cur is NULL, prev is the new head.

steps.title: A stack on an array
hints: `top` is both the count and the index of the next free slot.
push: if full return 0, else `s->items[s->top++] = v;`
pop: `return s->items[--s->top];`

modules.title: Bits and the preprocessor
modules.summary: Work with individual bits using bitwise operators and flags, and control compilation with #define and macros.

steps.title: #define constants
steps.text:
Lines starting with `#` are handled by the **preprocessor** before compilation. `#define` does a text substitution:

```c
#define MAX_ROUNDS 24
```

Every `MAX_ROUNDS` in the code is replaced with `24` before the compiler sees it. By convention macro names are UPPERCASE.

**Your turn:** define `TEAM_SIZE` as `5` so the program prints `10 players`.
hints: `#define NAME value`, with no `=` and no semicolon.

steps.title: Macro pitfalls
steps.text:
Macros can take arguments, but they're pure text replacement, which bites:

```c
#define SQUARE(x) x * x
SQUARE(1 + 2)   // becomes 1 + 2 * 1 + 2 = 5, not 9!
```

The fix: wrap every argument **and** the whole body in parentheses:

```c
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
```

**Your turn:** `DOUBLE(3 + 4) * 2` should be 28, but this prints 18. Fix the `DOUBLE` macro.
hints: Expand it by hand: `3 + 4 + 3 + 4 * 2` = 18. The `* 2` only grabbed the last 4.
Wrap the argument and the body: `#define DOUBLE(x) ((x) + (x))`.

require.message: Parenthesize the macro fully: `((x) + (x))`.

steps.title: Bitwise operators
steps.text:
Bitwise operators work on the individual bits of integers:

| Op | Name | Example (binary) |
|---|---|---|
| `&` | AND | `1100 & 1010 = 1000` |
| `\|` | OR | `1100 \| 1010 = 1110` |
| `^` | XOR | `1100 ^ 1010 = 0110` |
| `~` | NOT | flips every bit |
| `<<` | shift left | `0001 << 2 = 0100` |
| `>>` | shift right | `1000 >> 3 = 0001` |

`1 << n` is a number with only bit `n` set (that's 2 to the power n).

**Your turn:** write `int count_bits(unsigned x)` that returns how many bits are 1. Check the lowest bit with `x & 1`, then shift right.
steps.seed:
int count_bits(unsigned x) {

}
hints: Loop while x is not 0. Add `x & 1` to the count, then `x >>= 1`.

steps.title: Flags
steps.text:
Bits make compact on/off switches. Give each flag its own bit:

```c
#define HAS_HELMET  (1u << 0)
#define HAS_KIT     (1u << 1)
#define IS_SCOPED   (1u << 2)

unsigned state = 0;
state |= HAS_KIT;            // turn on
state &= ~HAS_KIT;           // turn off
state ^= IS_SCOPED;          // toggle
if (state & HAS_HELMET) {}   // test
```

**Your turn:** fill in the operators.

steps.title: Challenge: power of two
steps.text:
A classic bit trick: a positive number is a power of two exactly when it has a single 1 bit. And `x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so for powers of two it gives 0.

**Your turn:** write `int is_pow2(unsigned x)` returning 1 or 0, without loops.
steps.seed:
int is_pow2(unsigned x) {

}
hints: Zero is not a power of two, so handle it.

forbid.message: Solve it without a loop using `x & (x - 1)`.

modules.title: Files
modules.summary: Read and write real files. fopen modes, fprintf and fscanf, reading lines with fgets, handling errors, appending, safe formatting with snprintf, and a CSV report.

steps.title: Write a file, read it back
steps.text:
`fopen` opens a file and gives you a `FILE *` handle. The second argument is the **mode**:

| Mode | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"r"` | read; fails if the file doesn't exist |
| `"w"` | write; creates the file, or **empties** it if it exists |
| `"a"` | append; writes go to the end |

Then use `fprintf(f, ...)` exactly like `printf`, and always `fclose(f)` when you're done. Closing flushes buffered data to disk and frees the handle.

On this site, each run gets its own private, empty folder, so your program can create files freely.

**Your turn:** open `scores.txt` for writing, then for reading.
hints: Writing mode is `"w"` and reading mode is `"r"`. Include the double quotes: they're strings.

steps.title: Reading lines with fgets
hints: `while (fgets(line, sizeof line, f) != NULL)` loops over the lines.
Strip the newline with `line[strcspn(line, "\n")] = '\0';` before measuring.
Use `>` (not `>=`) so the first of equally long lines wins.

require.message: Read the file line by line with `fgets`.

steps.title: When fopen fails
hints: Open with `fopen(path, "r")` and return -1 if it's NULL.
Store fgetc's result in an **int**, not a char, so EOF can be told apart from a real byte: `int c; while ((c = fgetc(f)) != EOF)`.
Don't forget `fclose(f);` before returning the count.

steps.title: Loading records
steps.text:
Structured text files are everywhere: one record per line, fields separated by spaces or commas. `fscanf` reads fields straight into variables and returns **how many it matched**, which is how you detect both the end of the file and malformed lines.

```c
while (fscanf(f, "%31s %d", p.name, &p.score) == 2) { ... }
```

Always give `%s` a width (`%31s` for a 32-byte buffer), so a long word can't overflow the array.

**Your turn:** `roster.txt` holds `name score` pairs. Load them into the array (at most 32) and print the player with the highest score, then the average score with one decimal place.
hints: `while (n < 32 && fscanf(f, "%31s %d", team[n].name, &team[n].score) == 2) n++;`
Track the index of the best player and a running total while looping.
Divide as doubles for the average: `(double)total / n`, printed with `%.1f`.

steps.title: Appending
steps.text:
Mode `"a"` opens a file for **appending**: it's created if missing, and every write goes to the end, keeping what was there. That's exactly what log files need.

Other modes you'll meet:

| Mode | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `"r+"` | read and write an existing file |
| `"rb"`, `"wb"` | binary mode: no newline translation (matters on Windows) |

**Your turn:** write `int append_line(const char *path, const char *line)` that appends `line` plus a newline. Return 0 on success and -1 if the file can't be opened.
hints: Open with mode `"a"`, check for NULL, write with `fprintf(f, "%s\n", line);`, then fclose.

steps.title: Safe formatting with snprintf
hints: `int needed = snprintf(buf, size, "%s %d/%d", name, kills, deaths);`
It was truncated when `needed >= size` (compare as size_t after checking needed isn't negative).

forbid.message: Use `snprintf` with the buffer size, never plain `sprintf`.

steps.title: Challenge: a CSV report
steps.text:
A realistic batch job: read input data, aggregate it, write an output file.

`sales.csv` starts with a header line, then `region,amount` rows (amounts are whole dollars). **Your turn:**

1. Skip the header, then total the amounts per region (at most 10 regions, names up to 15 characters), keeping regions in the order they first appear.
2. Write `report.txt` with one `REGION TOTAL` line per region.
3. Then read `report.txt` back and print it, so the test can see what you wrote.

Tip: `sscanf(line, "%15[^,],%d", region, &amount)` reads everything up to the comma as the region, then the number.
hints: Keep two parallel arrays: `char names[10][16]` and `long totals[10]`, plus a count.
For each row, search names for the region. If it's new, add it with a total of 0. Then add the amount.
Read the header once with `fgets` before the loop so it isn't counted.
After writing and closing report.txt, reopen it with "r" and copy each line to stdout with `fputs`.

require.message: Write the results to `report.txt` (opened with mode "w"), then read that file back to print it.

files.sales.csv:
region,amount
eu,100
na,250
eu,40
asia,75
na,5

modules.title: Function pointers and callbacks
modules.summary: Treat functions as values. Function pointer syntax, typedefs, dispatch tables, qsort comparators, generic code with void*, and callbacks that carry context.

steps.title: Functions have addresses
steps.text:
A function lives in memory like everything else, so you can store its address in a **function pointer** and call it later:

```c
int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; }

int (*op)(int, int) = add;   // op points at add
printf("%d\n", op(2, 3));    // 5
```

Read `int (*op)(int, int)` as: "op is a pointer to a function taking (int, int) and returning int". The parentheses around `*op` matter: without them, `int *op(int, int)` declares a *function* returning `int *`.

**Your turn:** point `op` at `sub` and call it.
hints: A function's name used as a value is its address: `op = sub;`
Call through the pointer exactly like a function: `op(10, 4)`.

steps.title: typedef and passing callbacks
steps.text:
Function pointer types get unreadable fast, so give them a name with `typedef`:

```c
typedef int (*BinOp)(int, int);
```

Now `BinOp` is a type, and you can pass behavior into a function. The function you pass is called a **callback**:

```c
int fold(const int *a, int n, int init, BinOp f);
fold(a, n, 0, add);   // sum
fold(a, n, 1, mul);   // product
```

**Your turn:** write `fold`. It starts with `init` and combines it with each element in order: `acc = f(acc, a[i])`.
hints: `int acc = init;` then for each element `acc = f(acc, a[i]);`

steps.title: A dispatch table
hints: Write `static int mul(int a, int b)` and add `{"mul", mul},` to the table.
Loop over the table; when `strcmp(commands[i].name, name) == 0`, call `commands[i].fn(a, b)`.
Remember whether you found a match, and print `unknown %s` if not.

forbid.message: Look commands up in the table instead of comparing against each name by hand.

steps.title: Sorting with qsort
hints: Inside the comparator, convert: `const Player *a = pa, *b = pb;`
Higher score first means comparing b to a: `(b->score > a->score) - (b->score < a->score)`.
If the scores are equal, `return strcmp(a->name, b->name);`
`qsort(p, n, sizeof *p, by_score_desc);`

require.message: Sort with the standard `qsort` and your comparator.

steps.title: Generic code with void *
steps.text:
`qsort` works on any type because it treats the array as raw bytes: a `void *` base pointer plus an element `size`. Element `i` starts at byte offset `i * size`:

```c
const char *bytes = base;            // char * allows byte arithmetic
const void *elem = bytes + i * size;
```

You can't do arithmetic on `void *` itself in standard C, which is why you go through `char *`.

**Your turn:** write `find_first`, which returns a pointer to the first element for which `pred` returns nonzero, or `NULL`.
hints: Convert once: `const char *bytes = base;` Then element i is at `bytes + i * size`.
Call `pred(elem)` and return elem on the first nonzero result. After the loop, `return NULL;`

steps.title: Challenge: an event bus
steps.text:
A bare function pointer has no memory of its own. To let a callback update *your* data, C APIs pass a `void *ctx` ("context" or "user data") alongside it, and hand it back on every call:

```c
typedef void (*Handler)(int event, void *ctx);
```

That's how GUI toolkits, `pthread_create`, network libraries and game engines all do callbacks in C.

**Your turn:** build a tiny event bus that stores up to 8 handler/context pairs.

- `int bus_on(Bus *b, Handler h, void *ctx)`: register; returns 0, or -1 when full
- `void bus_emit(Bus *b, int event)`: calls every handler in registration order with the event and **its own** ctx
hints: bus_on: if `b->count >= MAX_HANDLERS` return -1. Otherwise store h and ctx at index count, then count++.
bus_emit: for each i, `b->handlers[i](event, b->contexts[i]);`

modules.title: Integer types and undefined behavior
modules.summary: How big each integer type really is, unsigned wraparound, signed overflow, fixed-width types, size_t traps, floating-point rounding, and the undefined behavior every C programmer must recognize.

steps.title: Sizes and limits
steps.text:
C only promises **minimum** sizes. On today's common platforms:

| Type | Usual size | Range (signed) |
|---|---|---|
| `char` | 1 byte | -128 to 127 |
| `short` | 2 bytes | about ±32 thousand |
| `int` | 4 bytes | about ±2.1 billion |
| `long` | 4 **or** 8 bytes | depends on the platform! |
| `long long` | 8 bytes | about ±9.2 × 10¹⁸ |

`long` is 8 bytes on 64-bit Linux and macOS, but 4 bytes on Windows and on 32-bit systems (including the WebAssembly this site runs on). Code that assumes one or the other breaks when it moves. That's why professional code uses the exact-width types you'll meet in a few steps.

`<limits.h>` gives the real limits for the platform you compile on: `INT_MAX`, `INT_MIN`, `LLONG_MAX`, `UINT_MAX`, `CHAR_BIT` (bits in a byte, 8 everywhere you'll ever work).

**Your turn:** print the largest `int`, then the smallest.
hints: The macros are `INT_MAX` and `INT_MIN`, from `<limits.h>`.

steps.title: Unsigned wraparound
steps.text:
Unsigned integers can't be negative. Their arithmetic is defined to **wrap around** modulo 2ᴺ: go below 0 and you land at the top.

```c
unsigned int x = 0;
x = x - 1;               // 4294967295, not -1
```

This is well-defined (unlike signed overflow, next step), and it's useful for hashing and bit manipulation. It's also a classic trap in countdown loops:

```c
for (size_t i = n - 1; i >= 0; i--)   // i >= 0 is ALWAYS true: infinite loop
```

The idiomatic safe countdown tests *before* decrementing:

```c
for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; )         // visits n-1, n-2, ..., 0
```

**Your turn:** read a count `n` and then `n` integers into an array (at most 100), and print them in **reverse** order on one line, separated by spaces. Use a `size_t` index for the reverse loop.
hints: `for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; )` checks i > 0 and *then* decrements, so the body sees n-1 down to 0.
Print a space after every number except the last one printed (when i is 0).

require.message: Count down with a `size_t` index, starting from `n`: `for (size_t i = n; i-- > 0; )`.

steps.title: Signed overflow is undefined
steps.text:
For **signed** integers, going past `INT_MAX` is **undefined behavior** (UB). "Undefined" doesn't mean "wraps around". It means the C standard puts *no requirements at all* on what happens, and optimizers rely on that. For example, the compiler may delete `if (x + 1 < x)` entirely, because in a program without UB that condition can never be true.

So you must check **before** the operation, using only operations that can't overflow:

```c
if (b > 0 && a > INT_MAX - b)  /* a + b would overflow upward */
if (b < 0 && a < INT_MIN - b)  /* a + b would overflow downward */
```

(GCC and Clang also offer `__builtin_add_overflow`, and C23 standardizes `ckd_add` in `<stdckdint.h>`. It's still worth knowing how to write the check yourself.)

**Your turn:** write `int checked_add(int a, int b, int *out)`. If the sum fits, store it in `*out` and return 1. Otherwise return 0 and leave `*out` untouched.
hints: Positive b: the sum overflows exactly when `a > INT_MAX - b`. That subtraction is safe because b > 0.
Negative b: the sum underflows exactly when `a < INT_MIN - b`.
Only compute `a + b` after both checks pass.

forbid.message: Write the check with plain `int` comparisons against INT_MAX and INT_MIN.

steps.title: Fixed-width types
steps.text:
`<stdint.h>` gives types with an **exact** size on every platform:

| Type | Size | Use it for |
|---|---|---|
| `int8_t` / `uint8_t` | 1 byte | raw bytes, pixels |
| `int32_t` / `uint32_t` | 4 bytes | file formats, protocols |
| `int64_t` / `uint64_t` | 8 bytes | big counters, hashes, timestamps |

Whenever data leaves the program (files, network packets, hashes), professional code uses these instead of `int` or `long`, so it means the same thing on every machine.

To print them portably, `<inttypes.h>` has format macros: `printf("%" PRIu64 "\n", x);`

**Your turn:** implement the 64-bit **FNV-1a** hash, a simple, widely used string hash:

```
hash = 14695981039346656037
for each byte b of the string:
    hash = hash XOR b
    hash = hash * 1099511628211      (wrapping, which uint64_t does for free)
```
hints: Start with `uint64_t h = 14695981039346656037ULL;`. The `ULL` suffix makes the constant unsigned long long.
Walk the string as `unsigned char` so bytes above 127 aren't negative: `(const unsigned char *)s`.

steps.title: The signed/unsigned comparison trap
steps.text:
When you compare a signed `int` with an unsigned value like `size_t` (what `strlen` and `sizeof` return), C converts the **int to unsigned** first. A negative int becomes a huge positive number:

```c
int n = -1;
if (strlen("abc") > n)   // false! -1 becomes 18446744073709551615 (or 4294967295)
```

`-Wall -Wextra` warns about this (`-Wsign-compare`). Treat that warning as a bug report, not noise.

**Your turn:** `longer_than(s, n)` should return 1 when `s` has more than `n` characters. It's wrong for negative `n` (every string is longer than -1 characters). Fix it without casting the length to `int` (strings can be longer than `INT_MAX`).
hints: Handle the negative case first: any string is longer than a negative length.
Once n is known to be >= 0, `(size_t)n` is safe: `return n < 0 || strlen(s) > (size_t)n;`

forbid.message: Don't cast the length to int; handle negative n first, then compare as size_t.

steps.title: Floating-point rounding
steps.text:
`double` stores numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions (like 0.1) have no exact binary form. So:

```c
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3    // false! 0.30000000000000004 vs 0.29999999999999998
```

Two rules professionals follow:

1. **Never compare doubles with `==`** after arithmetic. Check they're *close enough*, relative to their size.
2. **Never store money in `double`.** Store integer **cents** (`int64_t`), and only format as dollars for display.

A good closeness test scales the tolerance with the numbers:

```
|a - b| <= eps * max(1, |a|, |b|)
```

**Your turn:** write `int nearly_equal(double a, double b, double eps)` using that formula. Don't use `<math.h>`; write the absolute value yourself.
steps.seed:
int nearly_equal(double a, double b, double eps) {

}
hints: Write a tiny helper: `static double absd(double x) { return x < 0 ? -x : x; }`
scale starts at 1.0 and grows to |a| or |b| if either is bigger.
`return absd(a - b) <= eps * scale;`

steps.title: Challenge: hunt the undefined behavior
steps.text:
Undefined behavior is the biggest source of security holes in C. Learn to spot the usual suspects:

| UB | Example |
|---|---|
| Out-of-bounds access | `a[n]` in an array of n elements |
| Signed overflow | `INT_MAX + 1` |
| Reading uninitialized memory | `int x; printf("%d", x);` |
| Null or dangling pointer use | `*NULL`, use after `free` |
| Shifting too far | `1 << 32` on a 32-bit int |
| Modifying twice without sequencing | `i = i++ + 1;` |

The worst part: UB often *seems* to work, until a new compiler version, an optimization level or an input changes. On a real machine, `-fsanitize=address,undefined` catches most of these at runtime (the Pro Track covers it).

**Your turn:** these two functions each have undefined behavior. Fix both:

- `sum` reads one element past the end of the array.
- `midpoint` overflows for large inputs. Compute it without overflowing (assume `lo <= hi`).
hints: An array of n elements has indexes 0 to n - 1. The loop condition should be `i < n`.
`lo + (hi - lo) / 2` never overflows when lo <= hi, because `hi - lo` fits.

modules.title: Organizing programs
modules.summary: How real C programs are split into files. Headers and include guards, static and extern, const-correct APIs, command-line arguments, exit codes and stderr.

steps.title: Headers and include guards
steps.text:
Real C programs are split into many files. Each module has two parts:

- a **header** (`score.h`) with *declarations*: types, function prototypes, constants. It's the module's public interface.
- a **source file** (`score.c`) with the *definitions*: the actual function bodies.

Other files `#include "score.h"` to use the module. The compiler builds each `.c` file separately, then the **linker** joins them.

```c
/* score.h */
#ifndef SCORE_H
#define SCORE_H

typedef struct { int kills, deaths; } Score;
double kd_ratio(Score s);

#endif
```

That `#ifndef` / `#define` / `#endif` wrapper is an **include guard**. Headers often get included twice (a.h includes b.h, and so does main.c), and defining the struct twice is an error. The guard makes the second copy vanish.

The editor here holds a single file, so this program pastes the "header" in **twice** to simulate a double include. **Your turn:** complete the guard so it compiles.
hints: The guard is `#ifndef NAME`, then `#define NAME`, then the contents, then `#endif`.

steps.title: static functions and variables
steps.text:
`static` has two jobs in C, and both are about **hiding**:

1. On a function or global variable, it means **internal linkage**: the name is private to its `.c` file. Other files can't call it, and two files can each have their own `static int helper(void)` without clashing. Mark every helper that isn't part of the header `static`.
2. On a local variable, it means the variable **keeps its value between calls**. It's created once, not every time the function runs.

```c
static int clamp(int v) { ... }   /* private helper */

int next_id(void) {
    static int last = 0;          /* initialized once */
    return ++last;
}
```

**Your turn:** write `int next_ticket(void)` that returns 1, 2, 3, ... on successive calls, using a static local. Also write a private `static` helper `pad3(int n)` returning `n % 1000`, and use it so tickets wrap back to 0 after 999.
steps.seed:
int next_ticket(void) {

}
hints: `static int pad3(int n) { return n % 1000; }` goes above next_ticket.
Inside next_ticket: `static int last = 0; last = pad3(last + 1); return last;`

require.message: Define the helper as `static int pad3(int n)` so it's private to this file.
Keep the counter in a `static` local variable inside next_ticket.

steps.title: extern and shared state
steps.text:
A global variable **defined** in one file can be used from another by **declaring** it with `extern`:

```c
/* config.h */
extern int max_rounds;     /* declaration: "it exists somewhere" */

/* config.c */
int max_rounds = 30;       /* the one definition */
```

The declaration goes in a header; the definition goes in exactly one `.c` file. Two definitions is a linker error, and zero is an "undefined reference" error.

That said, mutable globals are a common source of bugs in large codebases: any code anywhere can change them, and they make testing hard. Prefer passing a struct pointer around. Globals are best kept `const`.

**Your turn:** declare `max_rounds` with `extern` above `main` so it can be used before the definition that appears later in the file.
hints: A declaration without a definition uses the `extern` keyword.

steps.title: const-correct interfaces
steps.text:
In a header, a function's signature is a **contract**. Mark every pointer parameter the function only reads as `const`:

```c
size_t count_alive(const Player *team, size_t n);   /* reads only */
void heal_all(Player *team, size_t n, int amount);  /* modifies */
```

Callers can then pass `const` data safely, and readers know at a glance which functions have side effects. Adding `const` later is painful because it ripples through every caller, so get it right from the start.

**Your turn:** fix the three signatures. The read-only ones need `const`; `heal_all` really does modify the team, so it must stay non-const.
hints: Add `const` before `Player *team` in the two functions that only read it.
find_by_name's `name` is also read-only: `const char *name`.

require.message: count_alive only reads the team: make it `const Player *team`.
find_by_name only reads both the team and the name: make them `const Player *team` and `const char *name`.

forbid.message: heal_all changes hp, so its team parameter can't be const.

steps.title: Command-line arguments
steps.text:
`main` can receive the words typed after the program name:

```c
int main(int argc, char **argv)
```

- `argc` is the argument count, **including** the program name.
- `argv[0]` is the program name; `argv[1]` to `argv[argc - 1]` are the arguments, as strings.

So `./sum 4 5 6` has `argc == 4` and `argv[2]` is `"5"`. Convert numbers with `strtol`, which also tells you where parsing stopped, so you can detect junk like `"12abc"`:

```c
char *end;
long v = strtol(argv[i], &end, 10);
if (*end != '\0' || end == argv[i]) { /* not a clean number */ }
```

**Your turn:** print the sum of all arguments. If any argument isn't a clean integer, print `bad number: ARG` and stop. The tests run your program with different arguments.
hints: Loop from `i = 1` (argv[0] is the program name) to `i < argc`.
`long v = strtol(argv[i], &end, 10);` then check `end == argv[i] || *end != '\0'` for junk.

require.message: Read the numbers from `argv`.

steps.title: Challenge: a real command-line tool
steps.text:
Command-line tools follow conventions that scripts and other programs rely on:

- Normal output goes to **stdout**; error messages go to **stderr** (`fprintf(stderr, ...)`), so they don't pollute output that's piped somewhere else.
- The **exit code** reports success: `0` means everything worked; nonzero means something failed. Scripts check it (`if ./tool; then ...`). `<stdlib.h>` names them `EXIT_SUCCESS` and `EXIT_FAILURE`.
- Keep going after one bad input when that's useful, but still report failure at the end.

**Your turn:** write `lines FILE...`, a tool that prints `COUNT NAME` for each file and a final `COUNT total` line. A file that can't be opened prints `lines: cannot open NAME` to **stderr**, is skipped, and makes the program exit with code **1** at the end (after the total). With no arguments at all, print `usage: lines FILE...` to stderr and exit with code **2**.
hints: No arguments: `fprintf(stderr, "usage: lines FILE...\n"); return 2;`
Keep an `int status = EXIT_SUCCESS;`. When a file fails, print to stderr, set status to EXIT_FAILURE and `continue`.
Print the total after the loop, then `return status;`

require.message: Error and usage messages go to stderr: `fprintf(stderr, ...)`.

`std::string` does what C strings made painful:

```cpp
std::string a = "de_";
std::string b = a + "dust2";      // concatenation with +
b.size();                          // length (7)
b == "de_dust2";                   // real comparison with ==
b[0];                              // 'd'

```

modules.title: References and functions
modules.summary: References as safer aliases, const& for cheap read-only parameters, overloading and default arguments.

steps.title: References are aliases
steps.text:
A **reference** is another name for an existing variable. Declare one with `&` after the type:

```cpp
int hp = 100;
int& ref = hp;   // ref IS hp
ref -= 30;       // hp is now 70
```

Unlike pointers, a reference must be initialized, can't be null, and can't be re-pointed later. No `*` or `->` needed to use it.

**Your turn:** make `alias` a reference to `money`, then spend 800 through it.
hints: A reference to int is written `int&`.

steps.title: Pass by reference
steps.text:
Reference parameters let a function modify the caller's variables with none of the pointer noise:

```cpp
void heal(int& hp) { hp = 100; }

int hp = 12;
heal(hp);        // no & at the call site
```

**Your turn:** write `void swap_values(int& a, int& b)`.
steps.seed:
void swap_values(int& a, int& b) {

}
hints: Same as the pointer version but without `*`. Use a temporary.

steps.title: const references
steps.text:
Passing a `std::string` or a big object by value **copies** it. Passing by reference avoids the copy, and adding `const` promises you won't modify it. This is the everyday C++ way to take read-only parameters:

```cpp
int count_spaces(const std::string& s);
```

Rule of thumb: small types (`int`, `double`, `char`) by value, everything bigger by `const&`.

**Your turn:** write `bool starts_with(const std::string& s, const std::string& prefix)` without using any library `starts_with`.
hints: If the prefix is longer than s, it can't match.
Compare `s[i]` and `prefix[i]` for every i below `prefix.size()`.

`"int " + std::to_string(n)`

steps.title: Default arguments
steps.text:
Parameters can have default values, used when the caller leaves them out. Defaults go at the **end** of the parameter list:

```cpp
void spawn(std::string name, int hp = 100, int armor = 0);
spawn("bot");            // hp 100, armor 0
spawn("bot", 50);        // armor 0
```

**Your turn:** write `std::string pad(const std::string& s, int width, char fill = ' ')` that adds `fill` characters on the **left** until the string is `width` long. Strings already that long are returned unchanged.
hints: Copy s, then keep adding `fill` to the front while it's shorter than width.

```cpp

```

steps.title: Challenge: a Clock class
steps.text:
**Your turn:** write a class `Clock` representing a round timer in seconds:

- `Clock(int seconds)` creates it
- `void tick(int s = 1)` subtracts seconds but never goes below 0
- `bool expired() const` is true at 0
- `std::string display() const` returns `M:SS`, like `1:55` or `0:07`

Minutes are `left_ / 60`, seconds `left_ % 60`. Add a leading "0" when seconds < 10.
`std::to_string(m) + ":" + ...` builds the text.

steps.title: Member initializer lists
steps.text:
A constructor's **initializer list** (after the `:`) builds each member directly. Assigning inside the body instead first default-constructs the member and then overwrites it.

```cpp
Player(std::string name, int hp) : name_(std::move(name)), hp_(hp) {}
```

Some members *must* be set in the initializer list, because they can't be assigned later:

- `const` members
- reference members
- members whose type has no default constructor

Members are always initialized in the order they are **declared in the class**, not the order you list them. `-Wall` warns when the two orders differ (`-Wreorder`), because reading a member that isn't built yet is a real bug.

**Your turn:** give `Player` a constructor `Player(const std::string& name, int max_hp)` that sets the const `name_`, sets `max_hp_`, and starts `hp_` at `max_hp_`. Use the initializer list for all three.
hints: The shape is `Player(const std::string& name, int max_hp) : name_(...), max_hp_(...), hp_(...) {}`.
List members in the same order they are declared: name_, max_hp_, hp_. Then `hp_(max_hp_)` is safe because max_hp_ is already built.

steps.title: Keeping invariants
steps.text:
An **invariant** is a rule that must be true for every object, at all times, from the outside. For a health bar: `0 <= hp <= max`.

This is the real reason for `private`: if only member functions can touch the data, only they can break the rule, and you check it in one place. Every constructor must *establish* the invariant and every member function must *preserve* it.

```cpp
void damage(int amount) {
    hp_ = std::max(0, hp_ - amount);   // never below 0
}
```

**Your turn:** write class `Health`:

- `Health(int max)`: max below 1 becomes 1; starts full
- `void damage(int n)` and `void heal(int n)`: negative amounts are ignored; hp stays within `0..max`
- `int hp() const`, `int max() const`, `bool alive() const`
hints: Constructor: `explicit Health(int max) : max_(std::max(1, max)), hp_(max_) {}`
`damage`: if n > 0, `hp_ = std::max(0, hp_ - n);`. `heal` is the mirror image with `std::min(max_, ...)`.

steps.title: Challenge: a Fraction class

A value type that always keeps itself in a clean form is a great exercise in invariants. **Your turn:** write class `Fraction` whose invariant is: **always fully reduced, denominator always positive**.

- `Fraction(int num, int den = 1)`: `Fraction(2, -4)` becomes `-1/2`. You can assume `den != 0`.
- `int num() const`, `int den() const`
- `Fraction plus(const Fraction& o) const` and `Fraction times(const Fraction& o) const`
- `std::string str() const`: `"3/4"`, or just `"2"` when the denominator is 1

`std::gcd(a, b)` from `<numeric>` gives the greatest common divisor (it handles negative numbers).

`gcd(0, d)` is `d`, so 0/5 becomes 0/1 automatically.
`plus` and `times` just build a new Fraction and let the constructor reduce it: a/b + c/d = (ad + cb) / bd.

hints: Signature: `IntArray(const IntArray& other)`.

steps.title: Copy assignment with copy-and-swap
steps.text:
Copy **assignment** (`a = b;` on an existing `a`) is harder than the copy constructor: `a` already owns memory that must be released, and `a = a;` must not destroy itself.

The standard trick is **copy-and-swap**:

```cpp
void swap(IntArray& other) noexcept {
    std::swap(data_, other.data_);
    std::swap(n_, other.n_);
}
IntArray& operator=(IntArray other) {   // by value: a copy is made here
    swap(other);                        // take the copy's guts
    return *this;                       // other's destructor frees our old data
}
```

Why professionals like it:

- It reuses the copy constructor, so there's no duplicated copying code.
- Self-assignment is automatically safe.
- If the copy throws (runs out of memory), `*this` is untouched. That's called the **strong exception guarantee**.

**Your turn:** write the member `swap` and the copy-and-swap `operator=`.

`IntArray& operator=(IntArray other) { swap(other); return *this; }` (note: other is taken **by value**).

steps.title: Challenge: a scope guard
steps.text:
RAII isn't only for memory. Any "undo" action (close a file, unlock a mutex, roll back a transaction, restore a setting) can be tied to a destructor, so it runs however the scope is left: normal end, early `return`, or an exception.

A **scope guard** holds a function and calls it in its destructor, unless you `dismiss()` it first (for example, because the operation succeeded and there's nothing to undo). Many large codebases have one; C++ proposals call it `scope_exit`.

`std::function<void()>` can hold any callable that takes no arguments, including a lambda.

**Your turn:** write class `ScopeGuard`:

- `explicit ScopeGuard(std::function<void()> f)`
- the destructor calls `f` unless dismissed
- `void dismiss()`
- it must not be copyable (two copies would run the action twice)
hints: Store the function in a `std::function<void()> f_;` and a `bool active_ = true;`.
The destructor: `if (active_ && f_) f_();`. `dismiss()` sets active_ to false.
Delete the copy constructor and copy assignment, like the Lock step.

modules.title: Operator overloading
modules.summary: Teach your own types to work with +, ==, <<, [] and <, so they read like built-in types.

steps.title: operator+
hints: The function for `-` is named `operator-`.

steps.title: operator== and !=
hints: `bool operator==(const Score& a, const Score& b)`
Compare only `t` and `ct`.

steps.title: Printing with operator<<
hints: Signature: `std::ostream& operator<<(std::ostream& os, const Score& s)`.
`return os << "T " << s.t << " - " << s.ct << " CT";`

steps.title: operator[]
hints: Slot 1 is index 0, so return `slots_[slot - 1]`.
Write both `std::string& operator[](int)` and a `const` version returning `const std::string&`.

steps.title: operator< and sorting
steps.text:
`std::sort` (from `<algorithm>`) orders anything that has a `<`. Define `operator<` and your own type becomes sortable:

```cpp
std::vector<Player> team = ...;
std::sort(team.begin(), team.end());
```

(Vectors are the next module; for now just know `team.begin(), team.end()` means "the whole vector".)

**Your turn:** define `operator<` for `Player` so sorting puts the **most kills first**, and for equal kills, the name alphabetically first.
hints: "Comes first" means "is less". a comes before b if a has **more** kills.
`if (a.kills != b.kills) return a.kills > b.kills; return a.name < b.name;`

modules.title: vector and string
modules.summary: std::vector, the dynamic array you'll use every day, and the most useful std::string operations.

steps.title: std::vector basics
steps.text:
`std::vector<T>` is a growable array that manages its own memory. It's everything you built by hand with `realloc`, done right.

```cpp
#include <vector>

std::vector<int> v = {3, 1, 4};
v.push_back(1);           // append: {3, 1, 4, 1}
v.size();                 // 4
v[0];                     // 3
v.back();                 // 1
v.pop_back();             // remove last
```

**Your turn:** fill in the blanks.
hints: Appending is `push_back`, the element count is `size()`.
The fourth element has index 3.

steps.title: Loop over a vector
steps.text:
Range-based for works on vectors. Use `const auto&` to avoid copying each element:

```cpp
for (const auto& x : v) { ... }
for (auto& x : v) { x *= 2; }     // & to modify in place
```

Pass vectors to functions by `const&` (read-only) or `&` (to modify). Passing by value copies the whole thing.

**Your turn:** write `std::vector<int> running_total(const std::vector<int>& v)` that returns the prefix sums. `{1, 2, 3, 4}` becomes `{1, 3, 6, 10}`.
hints: Start an empty result vector and a running sum.
For each element, add it to the sum and `push_back` the sum.

steps.title: Insert and erase
steps.text:
Positions in a vector are expressed with **iterators**. `v.begin()` points at the first element, and `v.begin() + i` at element i.

```cpp
v.insert(v.begin() + 1, 99);   // insert before index 1
v.erase(v.begin() + 2);        // remove index 2
v.clear();                     // remove everything
```

**Your turn:** write `void remove_at(std::vector<std::string>& v, int i)` that removes element `i` if it's a valid index and does nothing otherwise.
hints: Guard first: `if (i < 0 || i >= (int)v.size()) return;`
`v.erase(v.begin() + i);`

steps.title: 2D vectors
hints: Make the result with `cols` rows of `rows` ints each.
`t[c][r] = m[r][c];` in a nested loop.

steps.title: string search and substrings
steps.text:
Handy `std::string` members:

```cpp
std::string s = "de_dust2";
s.find("dust");        // 3 (index of first match)
s.find("zz");          // std::string::npos (not found)
s.substr(3, 4);        // "dust" (start, length)
s.substr(3);           // "dust2" (to the end)
```

**Your turn:** write `std::string map_name(const std::string& s)` that strips a prefix ending in the first `_`. `"de_dust2"` becomes `"dust2"`; a string without `_` is returned unchanged.
hints: `s.find('_')` gives the index, or `std::string::npos`.
`s.substr(pos + 1)` is everything after it.

steps.title: Challenge: split
steps.text:
**Your turn:** write `std::vector<std::string> split(const std::string& s, char sep)` that breaks a string at every `sep`.

- `split("a,b,c", ',')` gives `{"a", "b", "c"}`
- `split("a,,b", ',')` gives `{"a", "", "b"}` (empty pieces are kept)
- `split("", ',')` gives `{""}`
hints: Build the current piece character by character.
When you hit `sep`, push the current piece and clear it. After the loop, push the last piece.

modules.title: map, set and friends
modules.summary: Associative containers (map, set, unordered_map), pairs, and the stack and queue adapters.

steps.title: std::map
hints: Inside the loop: `count[w]++;`
After the loop, iterate with `for (const auto& [word, n] : count)` and print.

tests.name: Test 1
tests.stdin: rush b rush a b b

tests.name: Test 3
tests.stdin: eco force eco full full full eco

steps.title: Look up without inserting
hints: `auto it = prices.find(item);`
`it == prices.end()` means not found. Otherwise the value is `it->second`.

steps.title: std::set
steps.text:
`std::set<T>` holds **unique** values, **sorted**. Inserting a duplicate does nothing.

```cpp
std::set<int> s = {5, 1, 5, 3};   // {1, 3, 5}
s.insert(2);
s.contains(3);                     // true (C++20)
s.count(9);                        // 0
```

**Your turn:** write `std::vector<std::string> unique_sorted(const std::vector<std::string>& v)` that returns the distinct strings in sorted order.
hints: Construct a set from the vector's range to deduplicate and sort.
Then build a vector from the set's range: `std::vector<std::string>(s.begin(), s.end())`.

steps.title: unordered_map
steps.text:
`std::unordered_map` is a hash table: no ordering, but lookups are usually **O(1)** instead of O(log n). Same interface as `map` for `[]`, `find`, `contains`.

Classic use: remember things you've seen.

**Your turn:** write `std::pair<int, int> two_sum(const std::vector<int>& v, int target)` that returns the indexes `{i, j}` (with `i < j`) of two numbers adding up to `target`, or `{-1, -1}`. Do it in one pass: for each element, check whether `target - v[j]` was seen before.
hints: Map each value to its index as you go.
Before storing v[j], check `seen.find(target - v[j])`. If found, return `{that index, j}`.

steps.title: pair and tuple
hints: Structured bindings start with `auto`.
A pair's members are `first` and `second`.

steps.title: Challenge: balanced brackets
steps.text:
`std::stack<T>` gives you `push`, `top`, `pop` and `empty`. It's the right tool for matching brackets: push each opener, and each closer must match the most recent opener.

**Your turn:** write `bool balanced(const std::string& s)` for `()`, `[]` and `{}`. Other characters are ignored.
hints: Push opening brackets.
On a closing bracket, the stack must be non-empty and its top must be the matching opener. Pop it.
At the end, the stack must be empty.

modules.title: Streams and formatting
modules.summary: Parse text with stringstreams, format tables with iomanip, read and write files with fstream, and teach your own types to be read with operator>>.

steps.title: Parsing with istringstream
hints: Inside the loop: `std::istringstream in(line);` then `in >> name`.
`while (in >> x) total += x;` adds up however many numbers the line has.
Skip blank lines: if reading the name fails, `continue`.

require.message: Parse each line with a `std::istringstream`.

steps.title: Formatting tables with iomanip
steps.text:
`<iomanip>` controls how values are printed:

| Manipulator | Effect |
|---|---|
| `std::setw(n)` | pad the **next** item to width n (only the next one!) |
| `std::left`, `std::right` | alignment inside that width (sticky) |
| `std::fixed` + `std::setprecision(2)` | always 2 digits after the decimal point (sticky) |
| `std::setfill('0')` | pad with a character other than space (sticky) |

"Sticky" settings stay on the stream until you change them. `setw` resets after each item.

```cpp
std::cout << std::left << std::setw(8) << "ropz" << std::right << std::setw(6) << 1.25 << "\n";
```

**Your turn:** read `name kills deaths` rows and print a table: name left-aligned in 10 columns, kills and deaths right-aligned in 4 columns each, then the K/D ratio right-aligned in 6 columns with 2 decimals (use 0 deaths as 1 death).
hints: Set `std::fixed << std::setprecision(2)` once before the loop; they're sticky.
Per row: `std::left << std::setw(10) << name`, then `std::right` and `std::setw(4)` before kills, again before deaths, `std::setw(6)` before the ratio.
Compute the ratio as a double: `static_cast<double>(kills) / (deaths == 0 ? 1 : deaths)`.

require.message: Line up the columns with `std::setw`.

forbid.message: Use iostream manipulators on this step, not printf.

steps.title: Building strings with ostringstream
