hints: `std::ostringstream out;` then write each number, with `sep` before every number except the first.
Return `out.str()`.

steps.title: Reading files with ifstream
hints: `std::ifstream in(path); if (!in) return std::nullopt;`
Loop with `std::getline(in, line)` and push the non-empty lines, then `return lines;`.

steps.title: Writing files with ofstream
steps.text:
`std::ofstream` writes a file. By default it truncates (like `"w"` in C). Pass `std::ios::app` to append instead:

```cpp
std::ofstream out("log.txt", std::ios::app);
out << "round " << n << "\n";
```

Check the stream after writing if the data matters: disks fill up. `if (!out)` catches failed writes as well as failed opens.

**Your turn:** write `bool save_scores(const std::string& path, const std::map<std::string, int>& scores)` that writes one `name=score` line per entry (the map's order), replacing any existing file. Return whether everything succeeded.
hints: `std::ofstream out(path); if (!out) return false;`
Structured bindings make the loop tidy: `for (const auto& [name, score] : scores)`.
Return `static_cast<bool>(out)`, which is false if any write failed.

steps.title: Challenge: operator>> for your own type
hints: Signature: `std::istream& operator>>(std::istream& in, Point& p)`.
Read into locals: `char open, comma, close; int x, y;` and check the three characters.
On success assign `p = {x, y};`, otherwise `in.setstate(std::ios::failbit);`. Always `return in;`.

modules.title: Algorithms and lambdas
modules.summary: Stop writing loops by hand. sort, find_if, count_if, accumulate and transform, powered by lambdas.

steps.title: sort and reverse
steps.text:
`<algorithm>` works on **ranges** given as a pair of iterators, usually `v.begin(), v.end()`:

```cpp
std::sort(v.begin(), v.end());       // ascending
std::reverse(v.begin(), v.end());
auto it = std::max_element(v.begin(), v.end());   // iterator to the max
```

**Your turn:** sort the scores ascending, then reverse them so the best is first.
hints: The algorithms are `std::sort` and `std::reverse`, both taking `(begin, end)`.

steps.title: Lambdas
steps.text:
A **lambda** is an unnamed function you write inline:

```cpp
auto square = [](int x) { return x * x; };
square(5);   // 25
```

- `[]` is the **capture list** (more soon)
- `(int x)` are the parameters
- the return type is deduced

Lambdas shine as arguments to algorithms. Here `std::sort` takes a third argument: a comparison that says whether `a` should come before `b`.

**Your turn:** sort the words by **length**, shortest first.
hints: The lambda body needs to hand back its answer, like any function.
a comes first when it's shorter: `return a.size() < b.size();`

steps.title: find_if, count_if, any_of
hints: `std::count_if(kills.begin(), kills.end(), [](const std::string& k) { ... })`
`k.ends_with("_hs")` works in C++20. Or check the size and use `substr`.

require.message: Use `std::count_if` with a lambda.

steps.title: accumulate and transform
hints: Sum with `std::accumulate(hits.begin(), hits.end(), 0)`, cast to double, divide by size.
For transform, create `std::vector<int> out(hits.size());` first so there's room to write into.

require.message: Use `std::accumulate` for the sum.
Use `std::transform` for halving.

steps.title: Captures
steps.text:
A lambda can use variables from the surrounding scope if it **captures** them:

| Capture | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `[x]` | copy of x |
| `[&x]` | reference to x |
| `[=]` | copy everything used |
| `[&]` | reference everything used |

```cpp
int limit = 50;
auto big = std::count_if(v.begin(), v.end(), [limit](int x) { return x > limit; });

int total = 0;
std::for_each(v.begin(), v.end(), [&total](int x) { total += x; });
```

**Your turn:** write `std::vector<int> above(const std::vector<int>& v, int threshold)` that returns the elements greater than `threshold`, keeping their order. Use `std::copy_if` with `std::back_inserter(out)` and a lambda that captures `threshold`.
hints: `std::copy_if(v.begin(), v.end(), std::back_inserter(out), [threshold](int x) { return x > threshold; });`

require.message: Use `std::copy_if`.

steps.title: Erase with a condition
steps.text:
Removing elements that match a condition used to need the "erase-remove idiom". C++20 made it one call:

```cpp
std::erase_if(v, [](int x) { return x < 0; });   // C++20
// old way:
v.erase(std::remove_if(v.begin(), v.end(), pred), v.end());
```

**Your turn:** write `void drop_dead(std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>& players)` that removes players whose hp (the `int`) is 0 or less.
hints: `std::erase_if(players, [](const auto& p) { return p.second <= 0; });`

modules.title: More of the STL
modules.summary: The rest of the everyday toolbox. enum class, std::array, deque, priority_queue, iterators and iterator invalidation, and std::function callbacks.

steps.title: enum class
steps.text:
Plain C `enum` values leak into the surrounding scope and silently convert to `int`, so `if (team == RED_ALERT)` can compare unrelated things. C++'s **scoped enum** fixes both:

```cpp
enum class Side { T, CT };
Side s = Side::CT;         // must be qualified
int n = s;                 // error: no implicit conversion
int m = static_cast<int>(s);  // explicit is fine
```

Combine it with `switch`: compilers warn (`-Wswitch`, part of `-Wall`) when you forget to handle one of the values, which catches bugs whenever someone adds a new enumerator later.

**Your turn:** write `std::string to_string(Weapon w)` covering every value, and `int price(Weapon w)`: rifle 2700, sniper 4750, pistol 300.
hints: `switch (w) { case Weapon::Rifle: return "rifle"; ... }`
Add a `return` after the switch too, since the compiler can't be sure an enum holds only listed values.

require.message: Use a `switch` over the enum so the compiler can warn about missing cases.

steps.title: std::array
steps.text:
`std::array<T, N>` is a fixed-size array with the size in its type (you built one in the templates module). Compared with a C array it:

- knows its size (`.size()`),
- doesn't decay to a pointer, so functions receive the whole thing,
- can be copied, compared with `==` and returned from functions,
- has bounds-checked access with `.at(i)`, which reports an error instead of silently reading garbage.

Use it whenever the size is fixed and known at compile time.

**Your turn:** write `std::array<int, 3> podium(const std::vector<int>& scores)` returning the three highest scores, highest first. Missing places are 0. Don't modify the input.
hints: Copy the vector, then sort the copy descending with `std::greater<int>()`.
`std::array<int, 3> top{};` starts as all zeros. Fill as many places as you have scores.

steps.title: deque, the double-ended queue
steps.text:
`std::deque` supports fast `push_back`, `push_front`, `pop_back` **and** `pop_front`, which makes it perfect for queues and sliding windows. (`std::vector` can only add and remove cheaply at the back. Erasing its front shifts every element.)

```cpp
std::deque<int> d;
d.push_back(1);
d.push_front(0);     // 0 1
d.pop_front();       // 1
```

`std::queue` is just a restricted wrapper around a deque.

**Your turn:** write class `MovingAverage` that remembers only the last `n` values added and reports their average.
hints: Keep a `std::deque<int> window_` and a running `sum_`.
On add: push_back and add to the sum. If the window is now larger than n, subtract `front()` and `pop_front()`.

steps.title: priority_queue and top-k
steps.text:
`std::priority_queue` is a **heap**: `push` and `pop` cost O(log n), and `top()` is always the largest element (by default).

To keep the **k largest** values of a big stream, use a *min*-heap of size k: whenever it grows past k, pop the smallest. That's O(n log k) instead of sorting everything.

```cpp
std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>> minheap;  // top() is the smallest
```

The three template arguments are: element type, underlying container, comparison.

**Your turn:** write `std::vector<int> top_k(const std::vector<int>& v, int k)` returning the k largest values, largest first, using a min-heap of size at most k.
hints: Declare `std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>> heap;`
Push every value; when the size exceeds k, `pop()` removes the smallest.
Pop everything into a vector (smallest first), then `std::reverse` it.

require.message: Use a `std::priority_queue` min-heap.

forbid.message: Solve it with the heap rather than sorting.

steps.title: Iterators
hints: If `first == last` return last. Otherwise remember `It best = first;`
Loop over the rest; when `*best < *first`, set `best = first`. Using `<` only (not `>`) keeps the first maximum and needs only operator<.

forbid.message: Write the loop yourself on this step.

steps.title: Iterator invalidation
steps.text:
Changing a container can **invalidate** iterators, pointers and references into it. Using one afterwards is undefined behavior, and one of the most common C++ bugs in real code:

| Container | What invalidates |
|---|---|
| `vector` | `push_back` that reallocates: **everything**. `erase`: the erased element and everything after it |
| `deque` | inserting at either end invalidates iterators (but not references) |
| `list`, `map`, `set` | only iterators to erased elements |

The safe erase-while-looping pattern uses the iterator `erase` **returns** (the element after the removed one):

```cpp
for (auto it = v.begin(); it != v.end(); ) {
    if (dead(*it)) it = v.erase(it);   // don't ++ after erasing
    else ++it;
}
```

(For vectors, `std::erase_if(v, pred)` does this in one efficient call, as you saw in the algorithms module. The loop pattern is still what you need for `map` and for loops that do more than erase.)

**Your turn:** write `int remove_expired(std::map<std::string, int>& sessions, int now)` that erases every session whose expiry time is `<= now`, returning how many were removed. Use the loop pattern.
hints: Use a loop with no increment in its header: `for (auto it = sessions.begin(); it != sessions.end(); )`.
If expired: `it = sessions.erase(it); removed++;` else `++it;`

require.message: Continue from the iterator erase returns: `it = sessions.erase(it);`

steps.title: Challenge: callbacks with std::function
steps.text:
`std::function<R(Args...)>` holds **any** callable with that signature: a plain function, a lambda (including one with captures), or an object with `operator()`. It's C++'s answer to the C function-pointer-plus-`void*` pattern from the C modules, but type-safe.

```cpp
std::function<void(const std::string&)> handler = [&count](const std::string&) { count++; };
handler("boom");
```

**Your turn:** build an `EventBus` where handlers subscribe to named events:

- `int on(const std::string& event, std::function<void(const std::string&)> fn)` registers a handler and returns a unique id (1, 2, 3, ...)
- `bool off(int id)` unregisters; returns false if the id isn't registered
- `int emit(const std::string& event, const std::string& payload)` calls every handler for that event, in registration order, and returns how many ran
hints: Store a private struct `{int id; std::string event; std::function<void(const std::string&)> fn;}` in a vector.
`on` pushes a new entry with `++last_id_` and returns that id.
`off` finds the id with `std::find_if` and erases it. `emit` loops over entries whose event matches.

modules.title: Smart pointers
modules.summary: unique_ptr and shared_ptr own heap objects for you, so delete disappears from your code. Plus weak_ptr for non-owning links.

steps.title: unique_ptr
steps.text:
`std::unique_ptr<T>` (from `<memory>`) owns one heap object and deletes it automatically when the unique_ptr goes away. It's RAII for heap memory, and it costs nothing extra at runtime.

```cpp
auto p = std::make_unique<Player>("ropz", 100);
p->take_damage(30);     // use it like a pointer
// no delete needed, ever
```

**Your turn:** create the object with `make_unique` and access it through the pointer.
hints: `auto b = std::make_unique<Bomb>(...)`
Members are reached through a pointer with `->`.

steps.title: Unique means unique
steps.text:
A `unique_ptr` can't be **copied** (two owners would both delete). It can be **moved**, which transfers ownership and leaves the source empty (null):

```cpp
auto a = std::make_unique<int>(5);
// auto b = a;               // compile error: copying is deleted
auto b = std::move(a);       // ok: b owns it, a is now nullptr
```

Functions that take ownership accept `std::unique_ptr<T>` by value; callers must `std::move` into them.

**Your turn:** complete `Inventory::add`, which takes ownership of an item and stores it in the vector. Then `count()` and `total_value()`.
hints: A unique_ptr parameter can't be copied into the vector, so move it: `items_.push_back(std::move(item));`
Loop with `for (const auto& it : items_) t += it->value;`

steps.title: Returning ownership
hints: Return `nullptr` for invalid sites.
`return std::make_unique<std::string>("bomb " + site);`

steps.title: shared_ptr
steps.text:
`std::shared_ptr<T>` allows **several owners**. It keeps a reference count and deletes the object when the last owner goes away. `use_count()` shows how many owners there are.

```cpp
auto a = std::make_shared<int>(7);   // count 1
auto b = a;                          // copying is fine: count 2
```

Prefer `unique_ptr` by default. Reach for `shared_ptr` only when ownership is genuinely shared.

**Your turn:** make the program print `1 2 3 2` by filling in the blanks.
hints: `std::make_shared<int>(2)` creates it, `use_count()` reports the owners.
p2 is a third owner (a copy of map) until its block ends.

steps.title: weak_ptr
hints: `if (auto p = w.lock())` both locks and checks.
Inside, `*p` is the string.

modules.title: Move semantics
modules.summary: Why C++ can pass big objects around cheaply. lvalues vs rvalues, std::move, move constructors and the rule of five.

steps.title: Copies are expensive
steps.text:
Copying a `std::vector` with a million elements copies a million elements. But often the source is about to disappear anyway (a temporary, or a variable you're done with). In that case you can **steal** its internals instead: that's a **move**.

- An **lvalue** is something with a name that lives on (`v`).
- An **rvalue** is a temporary about to die (`make_vector()`, `a + b`).

`std::move(x)` doesn't move anything by itself. It *casts* `x` to an rvalue, which says "I'm done with x, you may steal from it".

After a move, the source is in a valid but unspecified state. Don't read its value; you may assign a new one.

**Your turn:** move `big` into `store` instead of copying it.
hints: Wrap it: `std::move(big)`.

steps.title: Write a move constructor
hints: Signature: `Buffer(Buffer&& other) noexcept`.
Copy the pointer and size from other, then set `other.data_ = nullptr;` and `other.size_ = 0;`.

steps.title: Move assignment and the rule of five
hints: Signature: `Buffer& operator=(Buffer&& other) noexcept`.
Guard with `if (this != &other)`, free your old data with `delete[] data_;`, steal, reset other.
End with `return *this;`.

steps.title: Return by value is free
steps.text:
Returning a local object by value doesn't copy it. When you return a temporary (`return Widget(...);`), C++17 **guarantees** the object is built directly in the caller's variable: no copy, no move. Returning a named local is almost always optimized the same way, and otherwise it's moved.

So write functions that return by value; don't return pointers or use out-parameters for performance.

**Your turn:** the `Tracker` struct counts copies. Write `Tracker make_tracker(int id)` so that creating one via your function performs **zero** copies. The test prints the copy count.
hints: Just `return Tracker(id);`. Guaranteed copy elision does the rest.

steps.title: Moved-from objects
steps.text:
After `b = std::move(a);`, what is `a`? For standard library types the rule is **valid but unspecified**:

- You **may** destroy it, assign it a new value, or call functions with no preconditions (`clear()`, `empty()`, `size()`).
- You **must not** rely on its value. A moved-from `std::string` is usually empty, but nothing promises that.

So the professional habit is: after moving from something, either stop using it or reset it explicitly.

```cpp
std::vector<std::string> batch = std::move(pending);
pending.clear();   // now it's definitely empty and ready to reuse
```

**Your turn:** write `std::vector<std::string> take_all(std::vector<std::string>& src)` that moves the whole contents out of `src` (no element copies) and leaves `src` definitely empty.
hints: `std::vector<std::string> out = std::move(src);` steals src's buffer in one go.
Then `src.clear();` so the caller gets a known state, and `return out;`.

require.message: Move the whole vector with `std::move(src)` instead of copying element by element.

steps.title: Sink parameters and emplace_back
steps.text:
When a function is going to **keep** a string (store it in a member or a container), take it **by value** and move it into place. This is called a *sink* parameter:

```cpp
explicit Player(std::string name) : name_(std::move(name)) {}
```

- Caller passes a temporary: it's moved in twice, zero copies.
- Caller passes a variable it still needs: exactly one copy, which is unavoidable.

For containers, `emplace_back(args...)` constructs the element **inside** the vector from constructor arguments, instead of building a temporary and moving it in.

```cpp
team.emplace_back("ropz");   // calls Player(std::string) in place
```

**Your turn:** give `Player` a sink constructor, and write `void recruit(std::vector<Player>& team, std::string name)` that adds a player using `emplace_back` and moves the name.
hints: Constructor: `explicit Player(std::string name) : name_(std::move(name)) {}`
recruit: `team.emplace_back(std::move(name));`

require.message: Add the player with `team.emplace_back(std::move(name));`
In the constructor, move the parameter into the member: `name_(std::move(name))`.

steps.title: Challenge: a move-aware log
steps.text:
Put it together. `std::exchange(obj, new_value)` from `<utility>` sets `obj` to `new_value` and returns the **old** value, moving where it can. It's the tidy way to "take" a member and leave it reset:

```cpp
return std::exchange(lines_, {});   // hand over the lines, leave an empty vector
```

**Your turn:** write class `Log`:

- `void add(std::string line)`: a sink; ignore empty lines
- `int size() const`
- `std::vector<std::string> flush()`: hand over all lines (no copies) and leave the log empty
hints: `add`: `if (!line.empty()) lines_.push_back(std::move(line));`
`flush`: `return std::exchange(lines_, {});`

modules.title: Templates
modules.summary: Write code once for many types. Function and class templates, constexpr, and if constexpr.

steps.title: Function templates
hints: It starts with `template <typename T>`.

steps.title: Templates over containers
steps.seed: #include <vector>
hints: Start with `template <typename T>` on the line before the function.
Loop and compare each element with `==`.

steps.title: Class templates
hints: `push` is `items_.push_back(v);`.
`pop` saves `items_.back()`, calls `items_.pop_back()`, and returns the saved value.

steps.title: constexpr
steps.text:
`constexpr` functions can run **at compile time** when given constant inputs. The result is baked into the program:

```cpp
constexpr int square(int x) { return x * x; }
static_assert(square(12) == 144);   // checked by the compiler!
int arr[square(3)];                 // array size known at compile time
```

**Your turn:** write `constexpr long long power(long long base, int exp)`. The tests include `static_assert`s, so if your function can't run at compile time, it won't even compile.
steps.seed:
long long power(long long base, int exp) {

}
hints: Add `constexpr` in front of the return type.
A simple loop multiplying `r` by `base`, `exp` times, works in constexpr functions.

steps.title: if constexpr
hints: `if constexpr (std::is_arithmetic_v<T>) { ... } else { ... }`
Without `constexpr`, the string branch would also be compiled for int and fail.

steps.title: Values as template parameters
steps.text:
Template parameters don't have to be types. A **non-type template parameter** is a compile-time value, usually a size:

```cpp
template <typename T, std::size_t N>
class Ring { T items_[N]; /* ... */ };

Ring<int, 8> r;    // N is 8, baked in at compile time
```

That's exactly how `std::array<int, 5>` works. The size lives in the **type**, so there's no heap allocation, and `Ring<int, 8>` and `Ring<int, 16>` are different types.

**Your turn:** write `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class FixedStack` backed by a plain array `T items_[N]`:

- `bool push(const T& v)`: returns `false` (and does nothing) when full
- `T pop()`: removes and returns the top (assume non-empty)
- `std::size_t size() const`, `bool full() const`
- `static constexpr std::size_t capacity() { return N; }`
hints: `push`: if `count_ == N` return false; otherwise `items_[count_++] = v;` and return true.
`pop`: `return items_[--count_];`

steps.title: Template specialization
steps.text:
Sometimes one type needs different behavior from the general template. A **full specialization** provides a replacement for exactly that type:

```cpp
template <typename T>
struct TypeName { static std::string get() { return "unknown"; } };

template <>
struct TypeName<int> { static std::string get() { return "int"; } };
```

`template <>` with empty brackets means "all the parameters are already fixed". The compiler picks the most specific match. This is how the standard library implements things like `std::hash<std::string>`, and how you add support for your own types to library templates.

**Your turn:** add specializations of `TypeName` for `double` (`"double"`), `bool` (`"bool"`) and `std::string` (`"string"`).
hints: Copy the `TypeName<int>` block and change the type and the returned text.
For strings, specialize on `std::string`: `template <> struct TypeName<std::string> { ... };`

steps.title: Challenge: a MinStack<T>
steps.text:
A classic interview question, now generic. **Your turn:** write `template <typename T> class MinStack` where **every** operation is O(1), including finding the minimum:

- `void push(const T& v)`
- `void pop()` (assume non-empty)
- `const T& top() const`
- `const T& min() const`: the smallest element currently in the stack
- `bool empty() const`

Hint for the O(1) min: alongside each value, remember what the minimum was at that point. Or keep a second stack of minimums.
hints: Keep two vectors: `items_` and `mins_`.
On push, also push onto `mins_` when the value is less than or equal to the current min.
On pop, if the value leaving equals `mins_.back()`, pop `mins_` too.

modules.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
modules.summary: Derived classes, virtual functions and override, abstract interfaces, and polymorphic containers.

steps.title: Inheritance
hints: `class Sniper : public Weapon`
The base class is initialized in the initializer list by name: `: Weapon("awp", 115)`.

steps.title: virtual and override
hints: Same signature as the base, plus `override`: `std::string attack() const override { ... }`.

require.message: Mark the derived functions with `override`.

steps.title: Abstract classes
hints: Each class needs `double area() const override { ... }`.

steps.title: Polymorphic containers
hints: Each derived class implements `int damage(int hits) const override`.
Shotgun: 0 for no hits, else `80 + 20 * (hits - 1)`.
Sum with `for (const auto& w : ws) t += w->damage(hits);`

steps.title: Virtual destructors
steps.text:
Without a virtual destructor, deleting a derived object through a base pointer only runs the **base** destructor. The derived part never gets cleaned up.

**Your turn:** the program should print:

```
+ base
+ derived
- derived
- base
```

but `- derived` is missing. Fix it with one keyword.
hints: The base class destructor needs to be `virtual`.

steps.title: Calling the base version, and protected
steps.text:
An override often wants to **extend** the base behavior, not replace it. Call the base version by naming it:

```cpp
std::string describe() const override {
    return Unit::describe() + " [elite]";
}
```

Access levels, one more time:

| Keyword | Who can use it |
|---|---|
| `public` | everyone |
| `protected` | the class **and classes derived from it** |
| `private` | only the class itself |

Use `protected` sparingly. Every protected member is part of the contract with all future subclasses, so it's as hard to change later as a public one.

**Your turn:** finish `Medic`. Its `describe()` returns the base description plus `" +heal"`, and `heal(Unit& u)` restores `u` by the protected `power_` amount (use `u.restore(...)`).
hints: `std::string describe() const override { return Unit::describe() + " +heal"; }`
`void heal(Unit& u) const { u.restore(power_); }`: Medic can read `power_` because it's protected.

require.message: Reuse the base text by calling `Unit::describe()` instead of rebuilding it.

steps.title: Composition over inheritance
steps.text:
Inheritance means **is-a**: a `Pistol` *is a* `Weapon`. For **has-a** relationships, use a member instead. That's *composition*:

```cpp
class Squad : public std::vector<Player> { };   // wrong: a squad isn't a vector
class Squad { std::vector<Player> members_; };   // right: a squad has members
```

Why composition is the default in professional code:

- The class controls its own interface. Inheriting from `std::vector` would expose `erase`, `clear` and everything else, letting callers break your rules.
- You can swap the member's type later without touching callers.
- Standard containers have no virtual destructor, so they aren't meant to be base classes at all.

**Your turn:** write class `Squad` that *has* a `std::vector<std::string>` of names, with a maximum size of 5:

- `bool add(const std::string& name)`: false if full or already in the squad
- `bool remove(const std::string& name)`: false if not found
- `int size() const`, `std::string roster() const` (names joined with `", "`, in join order)
hints: Use `std::find` from `<algorithm>` to check for duplicates and to locate a name to erase.
For the roster, add `", "` before every name except the first.

forbid.message: Don't inherit here. A squad *has* members; keep them in the private vector.

steps.title: Challenge: program to an interface
steps.text:
In enterprise code, the most valuable use of virtual functions isn't game units: it's **dependency injection**. A class depends on an abstract *interface* instead of a concrete service, and whoever creates it passes in the real thing.

```cpp
class Clock { public: virtual ~Clock() = default; virtual long now() const = 0; };
class Session { public: explicit Session(const Clock& c); /* uses c.now() */ };
```

Production code passes a clock that reads the system time. **Tests** pass a fake clock they control, so time-dependent logic can be tested instantly and reliably. The same idea covers databases, network clients and file systems.

**Your turn:** write `class RateLimiter` that takes a `const Clock&` and allows at most `limit` calls to `allow()` in any window of `window` seconds. `allow()` returns true and records the call if under the limit, otherwise false. A call at time `t` falls out of the window once `now() >= t + window`.
hints: Store `const Clock& clock_` and a `std::deque<long>` of call times.
In `allow()`: read `t = clock_.now()`, pop calls from the front while `t >= front + window_`.
Then if the deque holds `limit_` calls, return false; otherwise push t and return true.

modules.title: Modern C++ (17 and 20)
modules.summary: The features that make today's C++ pleasant. optional, variant, string_view, concepts, ranges and span.

steps.title: std::optional
hints: Handle an optional leading `-`, then require at least one more character.
Build the number digit by digit: `v = v * 10 + (c - '0');`. Any non-digit means `return std::nullopt;`.

steps.title: std::variant and std::visit
steps.text:
`std::variant<A, B, C>` holds exactly **one** of several types, and knows which. It's a type-safe union.

```cpp
std::variant<int, std::string> v = 5;
v = "hello";                               // now holds a string
std::holds_alternative<std::string>(v);    // true
std::get<std::string>(v);                  // "hello"
```

`std::visit` calls a function with whatever is inside. A lambda with an `auto` parameter handles every type:

```cpp
std::visit([](const auto& x) { std::cout << x; }, v);
```

**Your turn:** an `Event` is either a `Kill{attacker, victim}`, a `Plant{site}` or a `RoundEnd{winner}`. Write `std::string describe(const Event& e)` returning `"A killed B"`, `"bomb planted at X"` or `"round to W"`. Use `std::holds_alternative`/`std::get`, or `std::get_if`.
hints: `std::get_if<Kill>(&e)` returns a pointer to the Kill, or nullptr if e holds something else.
Careful: `"bomb planted at " + p->site` adds a char to a pointer. Wrap the literal in `std::string(...)` first.

steps.title: std::string_view
steps.text:
`std::string_view` is a lightweight, **non-owning** view of characters: a pointer plus a length. It accepts string literals, `std::string`s and substrings without copying anything, which makes it the modern choice for read-only string parameters.

```cpp
int count_upper(std::string_view s);
count_upper("AWP");            // no std::string is created
s.substr(1, 2);                // also a view, no copy
s.starts_with("de_");          // C++20
```

Danger: a view doesn't keep the text alive. Never return a view of a local string.

**Your turn:** write `std::string_view trim(std::string_view s)` that returns the view without leading and trailing spaces.
hints: `s.remove_prefix(1)` drops the first char of the view, `s.remove_suffix(1)` the last.
Loop while the view isn't empty and its front (or back) is a space.

steps.title: Concepts
steps.text:
A plain template accepts any type and fails with a wall of errors deep inside if the type doesn't fit. **Concepts** (C++20) state the requirements up front:

```cpp
#include <concepts>

template <std::integral T>
T gcd(T a, T b) { ... }       // only integer types allowed

gcd(12, 18);    // ok
gcd(1.5, 2.0);  // clear error: double doesn't satisfy integral
```

You can write your own with `requires`:

```cpp
template <typename T>
concept HasSize = requires(T t) { t.size(); };
```

**Your turn:** write `template <std::integral T> T gcd(T a, T b)` using Euclid's algorithm: while `b != 0`, replace `(a, b)` with `(b, a % b)`. The tests also check that calling it with a `double` is rejected.
steps.seed: #include <concepts>
hints: Write `template <std::integral T>` above the function instead of `template <typename T>`.
Loop: `T t = a % b; a = b; b = t;` until b is 0, then return a.

steps.title: Ranges
hints: `players | std::views::filter(...) | std::views::transform(...)` makes a lazy view.
The filter lambda captures `min_kills`; the transform lambda returns `p.first`. Then loop over the view and push_back.

require.message: Use `std::views::filter`.
Use `std::views::transform`.

steps.title: std::span
hints: Sum the first k elements, then slide the window one step at a time.
Sliding: add the element entering the window and subtract the one leaving it.

modules.title: Handling errors
modules.summary: How to report failure without crashing. assert for bugs, error codes and optional for expected failures, a Result type, and how exceptions fit in.

steps.title: Bugs vs expected failures
hints: The header is `<cassert>` and the macro is `assert`.

steps.title: Status codes
steps.seed:
bool divide(int a, int b, int& out) {

}
hints: Return `false` first if `b == 0`.
Otherwise `out = a / b; return true;`. Put `[[nodiscard]]` before the return type.

steps.title: optional for "maybe"
steps.text:
When the only failure is "no result", `std::optional` says it clearly in the return type and forces the caller to check.

**Your turn:** write `std::optional<std::size_t> find_player(const std::vector<std::string>& team, const std::string& name)` returning the index or `std::nullopt`.
hints: Loop over the indexes and `return i;` on a match (it converts to optional).
After the loop, `return std::nullopt;`.

steps.title: A Result type
hints: Return a Result with braces: `return {std::nullopt, "missing $"};` or `return {value, ""};`.
Check the `$` first, then that there is at least one character after it, then parse digits.
Stop growing the number once it passes 16000, otherwise very long inputs overflow an int.

steps.title: Passing errors up
steps.text:
Real programs are layers: `main` calls `load_config`, which calls `parse_line`, which calls `parse_int`. When the bottom layer fails, each layer above has two honest choices:

1. **Handle it** (use a default, retry, skip the item), or
2. **Pass it up** unchanged, usually with an early `return`.

The one dishonest choice is swallowing it: returning a made-up value as if nothing went wrong. That's how bugs travel far from where they started.

```cpp
auto n = parse_int(part);
if (!n) return std::nullopt;   // pass it up
total += *n;
```

**Your turn:** `parse_int` is written for you. Write `std::optional<int> sum_csv(std::string_view s)` that sums comma-separated integers like `"3,4,-2"`. If **any** part fails to parse, the whole sum fails.
hints: Loop: find the next comma with `s.find(',')`, parse `s.substr(0, comma)`, then `s.remove_prefix(comma + 1)`.
If `parse_int` returns nullopt, immediately `return std::nullopt;`.
When `find` returns `std::string_view::npos`, that was the last part.

steps.title: Challenge: load a config
steps.text:
Put the pieces together in the kind of code every service has: a config loader that reports **precise** errors, because "invalid config" with no line number wastes everyone's time.

**Your turn:** write `ConfigResult load_config(const std::string& text)`. The text has one `key=value` per line:

- blank lines and lines starting with `#` are skipped
- a line with no `=` fails with `"line N: missing ="`
- an empty key fails with `"line N: empty key"`
- a key seen twice fails with `"line N: duplicate key KEY"`
- otherwise every pair goes into `values`

Lines are numbered from 1. Stop at the first error.
hints: Read lines with `std::istringstream in(text);` and `while (std::getline(in, line))`, counting as you go.
Skip empty lines and lines where `line[0] == '#'`.
`line.find('=')` gives the split point; key is `substr(0, eq)`, value is `substr(eq + 1)`.
Return `{{}, "line " + std::to_string(n) + ": missing ="}` style results on errors.

modules.title: Writing iterators and containers
modules.summary: Make your own types work with range-for and the standard algorithms. begin and end, writing an iterator class, const iteration, iterator concepts, lazy ranges and a ring buffer.

steps.title: Making a class iterable
hints: `int* begin() { return scores_; }` and `int* end() { return scores_ + count_; }`
The const versions are the same but return `const int*` and are marked `const`.

steps.title: Writing an iterator class
hints: `int& operator*() const { return node_->value; }`
`Iterator& operator++() { node_ = node_->next.get(); return *this; }`
`begin()` wraps `head_.get()`; `end()` wraps `nullptr`.

steps.title: Iterator concepts and algorithms
hints: Add `using iterator_category = std::forward_iterator_tag;`, `using value_type = int;` and `using difference_type = std::ptrdiff_t;`.
Add `Iterator() = default;` so it can be default-constructed.
Post-increment takes a dummy int: `Iterator operator++(int) { Iterator old = *this; --v_; return old; }`

steps.title: A lazy range
steps.text:
An iterator doesn't have to point at stored data at all. It can **compute** values on the fly. That's how `std::views::iota` works, and it's how Python's `range()` is built: no array is ever allocated, so `range(0, 1'000'000'000)` costs nothing.

**Your turn:** write `class Range` for `for (int i : Range(start, stop, step))` with a positive step, like Python: it yields start, start + step, ... while the value is `< stop`. Careful: with a step of 3, the values may jump **past** `stop` without ever equalling it, so the end condition can't be a plain `==` on the current value.
hints: Give Range a nested `Iterator` holding the current value and the step.
Compute how many values there are: `n = (stop - start + step - 1) / step` (or 0 if start >= stop). Then `end()` is at `start + n * step`, a value begin really reaches.
Alternatively, make `operator==` treat 'at or past stop' as equal to end. Either way, `for` must stop.

steps.title: Challenge: a ring buffer
steps.text:
A **ring buffer** (circular buffer) is a fixed-capacity queue stored in an array: the write position wraps around to the start, overwriting the oldest item when full. Audio pipelines, loggers and network stacks use them because they never allocate after construction.

```
capacity 4, after pushing 1..6:   [5][6][3][4]   oldest = 3
                                          ^head
```

**Your turn:** write `template <typename T, std::size_t N> class RingBuffer` with:

- `void push(const T& v)`: adds v; when full, overwrites the oldest
- `std::size_t size() const`, `bool full() const`
- `const T& operator[](std::size_t i) const`: i-th element counting from the **oldest**
- `begin()`/`end()` so range-for visits oldest to newest (an iterator holding a buffer pointer and an index works well)
hints: When not full, write at `(head_ + size_) % N` and grow size_. When full, overwrite `data_[head_]` and advance head_.
`operator[](i)` is `data_[(head_ + i) % N]`.
The iterator can store a pointer to the buffer and a logical index 0..size_; `operator*` returns `(*rb_)[i_]`.

modules.title: Variadic templates and type traits
modules.summary: Generic code at library level. Parameter packs and fold expressions, perfect forwarding, type traits, writing your own trait, constraining templates with concepts, and compile-time computation.

steps.title: Parameter packs and fold expressions
steps.text:
A **variadic template** accepts any number of arguments, of any types, as a *parameter pack*:

```cpp
template <typename... Ts>
auto sum(Ts... xs) {
    return (xs + ...);      // a fold expression: x1 + (x2 + (x3 + ...))
}
sum(1, 2, 3);        // 6
sum(1.5, 2);         // 3.5
```

`sizeof...(xs)` gives the number of arguments. Fold expressions work with any binary operator: `(xs && ...)`, `(... , f(xs))` and so on. `std::make_unique`, `std::tuple`, `emplace_back` and `std::format` are all built on packs.

**Your turn:** write `count_if_all(pred, xs...)`, returning how many of the arguments satisfy `pred`, and `all_positive(xs...)`. Use fold expressions, no loops.
hints: A binary fold with an initial value handles the empty pack: `(0 + ... + expr)`.
For each argument, `expr` can be `(pred(xs) ? 1 : 0)`.
`((xs > 0) && ...)` is true for an empty pack.

forbid.message: Use fold expressions instead of loops.

steps.title: Perfect forwarding
steps.text:
A factory like `std::make_unique<T>(args...)` must pass its arguments to `T`'s constructor **exactly** as received: temporaries as rvalues (so they can be moved), named variables as lvalues (so they're copied, not stolen).

That's **perfect forwarding**:

```cpp
template <typename T, typename... Args>
std::unique_ptr<T> make(Args&&... args) {
    return std::unique_ptr<T>(new T(std::forward<Args>(args)...));
}
```

- `Args&&` in a template is a **forwarding reference**: it binds to anything and remembers whether it was an lvalue or an rvalue.
- `std::forward<Args>(args)...` restores that category when passing it on.

**Your turn:** write `template <typename T, typename... Args> T& emplace_into(std::vector<T>& v, Args&&... args)` that constructs a T at the end of v from the forwarded arguments (with `emplace_back`) and returns a reference to it.
hints: `emplace_back` returns a reference to the new element in C++17 and later.
`return v.emplace_back(std::forward<Args>(args)...);`

require.message: Forward the arguments: `std::forward<Args>(args)...`

steps.title: Type traits
hints: Chain `if constexpr ... else if constexpr ...` and check `std::is_same_v<T, bool>` first.
`std::is_signed_v<T>` tells signed from unsigned integral types.

steps.title: Writing your own trait
steps.text:
A trait is just a template struct with a `value`, where **specializations** give the answers. The standard ones are written exactly like this:

```cpp
template <typename T>
struct is_vector : std::false_type {};          // default: no

template <typename T, typename A>
struct is_vector<std::vector<T, A>> : std::true_type {};   // any vector: yes

template <typename T>
inline constexpr bool is_vector_v = is_vector<T>::value;
```

The second one is a **partial specialization**: it's still a template (over T and the allocator A), but only matches vectors.

**Your turn:** write the `is_vector` trait and `is_vector_v`, then use it in `size_of(const T& x)`: for a vector, return its `size()`; for anything else, return 1.
hints: Primary template inherits `std::false_type`; the partial specialization for `std::vector<T, A>` inherits `std::true_type`.
`template <typename T> inline constexpr bool is_vector_v = is_vector<T>::value;`
In size_of, `if constexpr (is_vector_v<T>) return x.size(); else return 1;`

steps.title: Constraining templates with concepts
hints: `template <typename T> concept Shape = requires(const T& s) { ... };`
Inside: `{ s.area() } -> std::convertible_to<double>;` and the same for name() with std::string.
Then `template <Shape S> double total_area(const std::vector<S>& shapes)` just loops and adds.

steps.title: Challenge: compile-time computation
steps.text:
`constexpr` functions can run **during compilation** when their inputs are constants. The result is baked into the program as a literal, and `static_assert` can check it. Lookup tables, hashes of fixed strings, unit conversions and configuration validation are often done this way in performance-critical code.

Since C++20, constexpr functions may use loops, local variables, `std::array` and even `std::vector` (as long as it doesn't escape).

**Your turn:**

- `constexpr std::array<int, N> first_primes<N>()`: the first N primes
- `constexpr std::uint32_t hash32(std::string_view s)`: 32-bit FNV-1a (start `2166136261u`, for each byte `h ^= byte; h *= 16777619u;`)

Both must work at compile time: the tests use them inside `static_assert`.
hints: first_primes: fill a `std::array<int, N> out{}` by testing n = 2, 3, 4, ... for divisors up to sqrt(n).
hash32: `std::uint32_t h = 2166136261u;` then for each char `h ^= static_cast<unsigned char>(c); h *= 16777619u;`.

modules.title: Formatting, time and text
modules.summary: The modern standard library for everyday service code. std::format and custom formatters, chrono durations, measuring time, strict number parsing with from_chars, and a log formatter.

steps.title: std::format
steps.text:
C++20's `std::format` combines printf's compactness with type safety: `{}` placeholders are filled in order, and the format is checked **at compile time** when it's a literal.

```cpp
std::format("{} has {} kills", name, k);        // "ropz has 25 kills"
std::format("{:>8}", "ab");                     // right-align in 8: "      ab"
std::format("{:<8}|", "ab");                    // left-align: "ab      |"
std::format("{:^7}", "mid");                    // center: "  mid  "
std::format("{:.2f}", 3.14159);                 // "3.14"
std::format("{:05}", 42);                       // zero-pad: "00042"
std::format("{:x} {:b}", 255, 5);               // hex and binary: "ff 101"
```

The spec after the colon is `[fill][align][width][.precision][type]`.

**Your turn:** write `std::string row(const std::string& name, int kills, double kd)` producing the name left-aligned in 10 characters, kills right-aligned in 4, and the K/D right-aligned in 6 with 2 decimals. Use a single `std::format` call.
hints: Three placeholders: `{:<10}`, `{:>4}` and `{:>6.2f}`.
`return std::format("{:<10}{:>4}{:>6.2f}", name, kills, kd);`

require.message: Build the row with `std::format`.

steps.title: Formatting your own types
hints: `template <> struct std::formatter<Money> : std::formatter<std::string> { ... };`
Inside `format`, build the text with `std::format("${}.{:02}", m.cents / 100, m.cents % 100)`.
Pass it on: `return std::formatter<std::string>::format(text, ctx);`

steps.title: chrono durations
steps.text:
Passing time around as a bare `int` invites bugs: seconds or milliseconds? `<chrono>` puts the unit **in the type**:

```cpp
using namespace std::chrono_literals;
std::chrono::milliseconds t = 1500ms;
std::chrono::seconds s = 2min;                              // exact conversions are implicit
auto whole = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::seconds>(t);   // lossy ones need a cast: 1s
t += 3s;                                                    // mixed units just work: 4500ms
```

Converting to a coarser unit truncates (1500ms becomes 1s), so the language makes you say `duration_cast` explicitly. `.count()` gives the raw number when you really need it, for example to print.

**Your turn:** write `std::string mmss(std::chrono::milliseconds t)` that formats a round timer as `M:SS` (truncating the milliseconds), like `1:55` or `0:07`.
hints: `auto m = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::minutes>(t);`
The leftover seconds: `duration_cast<std::chrono::seconds>(t - m)`.
`std::format("{}:{:02}", m.count(), s.count())`.

require.message: Convert units with `std::chrono::duration_cast` instead of dividing by 60000 by hand.

steps.title: Measuring time
steps.text:
`<chrono>` has several clocks, and picking the wrong one is a classic bug:

| Clock | Use it for |
|---|---|
| `std::chrono::steady_clock` | measuring elapsed time: it never jumps backwards |
| `std::chrono::system_clock` | wall-clock time ("now" as a date); can jump when the OS adjusts the time |

Timing code with `system_clock` can give **negative** durations if the clock is corrected mid-measurement. Always use `steady_clock` for intervals, timeouts and benchmarks:

```cpp
auto start = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
work();
auto elapsed = std::chrono::steady_clock::now() - start;   // a duration
```

**Your turn:** write `template <typename F> std::chrono::microseconds time_it(F&& f)` that calls `f()` once and returns how long it took.
hints: Take `std::chrono::steady_clock::now()` before and after calling `f()`.
Subtracting two time points gives a duration; `duration_cast` it to microseconds.

require.message: Measure intervals with `std::chrono::steady_clock`.

steps.title: Strict number parsing with from_chars
hints: `auto [ptr, ec] = std::from_chars(s.data(), s.data() + s.size(), v);`
Succeed only if `ec == std::errc()` **and** ptr reached the end of s.

require.message: Parse with `std::from_chars`.

steps.title: Challenge: a log formatter
steps.text:
Every service writes logs, and consistent, sortable, greppable log lines matter when you're debugging production at 3 a.m.

**Your turn:** write `std::string log_line(Level level, std::chrono::milliseconds uptime, std::string_view msg)` producing:

```
[HH:MM:SS.mmm] LEVEL message
```

- the uptime as zero-padded hours, minutes, seconds and milliseconds (hours can exceed 24)
- the level name (`DEBUG`, `INFO`, `WARN`, `ERROR`) left-aligned in 5 characters
- one space, then the message

Example: `log_line(Level::Warn, 65250ms, "disk 91%")` is `[00:01:05.250] WARN  disk 91%`.
hints: Peel off units with duration_cast: hours, then minutes from what's left, then seconds; the remainder is milliseconds.
A switch turns the enum into its name.

modules.title: Design patterns in modern C++
modules.summary: The patterns you'll meet in every large C++ codebase, written the modern way. Strategies as closures, a factory registry, observers with weak_ptr, pimpl, RAII wrappers for C libraries, and a table-driven state machine.

steps.title: Strategies as closures
hints: `return [pct](long cents) { return cents - cents * pct / 100; };`
flat_off: return 0 when the amount is bigger than the total.
total(): sum the prices, then `return discount(sum);`

steps.title: A factory registry
steps.text:
A **factory** creates objects by *name* (from a config file, a network message, a command line), returning them through a base-class pointer. Instead of a giant `if`/`else` chain, large codebases use a **registry**: a map from name to a creator function. New types register themselves without anyone editing the factory.

```cpp
using Creator = std::function<std::unique_ptr<Weapon>()>;
std::map<std::string, Creator> creators_;
```

Returning `std::unique_ptr` makes ownership obvious: the caller owns the new object.

**Your turn:** implement `Factory::add` (returns false if the name is already registered), `Factory::create` (returns `nullptr` for unknown names) and `Factory::names` (sorted).
hints: `creators_.emplace(name, std::move(make)).second` is false when the key already existed.
create: `find` the name; if missing return nullptr, otherwise call the creator: `it->second()`.
std::map is already sorted by key, so names() just collects the keys.

steps.title: Observers with weak_ptr
steps.text:
In the **Observer** pattern a subject notifies listeners when something happens. The hard part in C++ is **lifetime**: if a listener is destroyed while the subject still holds a pointer to it, the next notification uses a dangling pointer.

Storing `std::weak_ptr` solves it. The subject doesn't keep listeners alive, and `lock()` tells you whether each one still exists:

```cpp
for (auto& w : listeners_) {
    if (auto l = w.lock()) l->on_event(e);    // still alive: notify
}
```

**Your turn:** implement `Scoreboard::subscribe` and `Scoreboard::publish`. `publish` notifies every living listener in subscription order, **removes** expired ones, and returns how many were notified.
hints: subscribe: `listeners_.push_back(l);` converts the shared_ptr to a weak_ptr.
publish: loop with an iterator; `if (auto l = it->lock())` notify and advance, else `it = listeners_.erase(it);`

steps.title: Pimpl
hints: `struct Roster::Impl { std::vector<std::string> names; };`
`Roster::Roster() : impl_(std::make_unique<Impl>()) {}`, and `Roster::~Roster() = default;` after Impl is defined.
`Roster::Roster(Roster&&) noexcept = default;` also needs Impl complete, so it goes here too.

steps.title: RAII wrappers for C libraries
hints: `struct FileCloser { void operator()(std::FILE* f) const { if (f) std::fclose(f); } };`
`using File = std::unique_ptr<std::FILE, FileCloser>;` and open_file returns `File(std::fopen(path.c_str(), mode))`.
In first_line, `fgets` into a buffer, build a std::string and drop a trailing '\n'.

forbid.message: Let the File's deleter close the handle; don't call fclose by hand in first_line.

steps.title: Challenge: a table-driven state machine
steps.text:
Protocols, UI flows, order pipelines and game rounds are **state machines**. Encoding the legal transitions in a **table** (instead of nested ifs scattered through the code) makes them easy to review, test and extend:

```cpp
struct Transition { State from; Event on; State to; };
constexpr Transition table[] = {
    {State::Idle, Event::Start, State::Warmup},
    ...
};
```

**Your turn:** implement a match lifecycle with these transitions:

| From | Event | To |
|---|---|---|
| Idle | Start | Warmup |
| Warmup | GoLive | Live |
| Live | Pause | Paused |
| Paused | Resume | Live |
| Live | End | Over |
| Paused | End | Over |

Write `std::optional<State> next(State s, Event e)` using a table, and class `Match` whose `bool handle(Event e)` applies a legal event (returning true) or rejects an illegal one (returning false, state unchanged). `state()` returns the current state and `history()` the number of accepted events.
hints: Define `struct Transition { State from; Event on; State to; };` and a `constexpr Transition kTable[]` with the six rows.
next: loop over the table and return `t.to` on a match; otherwise `std::nullopt`.
handle: ask next(); if it's empty return false, otherwise update the state and count.

modules.title: Complexity and searching
modules.summary: Big-O in practice. Trading memory for speed with hash sets, binary search and lower_bound, two pointers, prefix sums and sliding windows, with tests big enough that slow solutions time out.

steps.title: Big-O in practice
steps.text:
**Big-O** describes how running time grows with the input size n, ignoring constant factors:

| Complexity | n = 1,000 | n = 1,000,000 | Typical example |
|---|---|---|---|
| O(1) | 1 | 1 | array index, hash lookup |
| O(log n) | 10 | 20 | binary search |
| O(n) | 1,000 | 1,000,000 | one pass over the data |
| O(n log n) | 10,000 | 20,000,000 | good sorting |
| O(n²) | 1,000,000 | 1,000,000,000,000 | comparing every pair |

A computer does roughly 10⁸ to 10⁹ simple operations per second. So at a million items, O(n²) takes **hours** while O(n log n) takes milliseconds. Interviews test this, and so does production traffic.

The most common fix for O(n²) is trading memory for time: remember what you've seen in a hash set, which has O(1) average lookup.

**Your turn:** write `bool has_duplicate(const std::vector<int>& v)` in O(n). The hidden test uses 200,000 numbers, so comparing every pair will run out of time.
hints: Keep a `std::unordered_set<int> seen;`.
`seen.insert(x).second` is false when x was already there. That's your duplicate.

steps.title: Binary search
steps.text:
In a **sorted** array, binary search finds a value in O(log n) by halving the search range each step. A million elements takes at most 20 steps.

```
lo = 0, hi = n - 1
while lo <= hi:
    mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2      (not (lo + hi) / 2: that can overflow!)
    if v[mid] == target: found
    if v[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1
    else: hi = mid - 1
```

Binary search is famously easy to get subtly wrong. Off-by-one errors in `lo`/`hi` cause infinite loops or missed elements. Write it carefully once and understand every `+ 1` and `- 1`.

**Your turn:** write `int find_index(const std::vector<int>& v, int target)` returning the index of `target` in the sorted vector `v`, or -1. Don't use the standard library's search functions.
hints: Track an inclusive range `lo..hi`, starting at 0 and size - 1.
`int mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2;` then move lo to `mid + 1` or hi to `mid - 1`.
The loop runs while `lo <= hi`; if it ends, the target isn't there.

forbid.message: Write the halving loop yourself on this step.

steps.title: lower_bound and upper_bound
steps.text:
In real code, use the standard library's binary searches on sorted ranges:

- `std::lower_bound(b, e, x)`: first element **not less than** x (where x would be inserted)
- `std::upper_bound(b, e, x)`: first element **greater than** x
- `std::binary_search(b, e, x)`: just yes or no

So the elements equal to x are exactly `[lower_bound, upper_bound)`, and the count of values in a range `[lo, hi]` is `upper_bound(hi) - lower_bound(lo)`, in O(log n) no matter how many there are.

**Your turn:** write `long count_in_range(const std::vector<int>& sorted, int lo, int hi)` counting values `v` with `lo <= v <= hi`.
hints: `auto first = std::lower_bound(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), lo);`
`auto last = std::upper_bound(sorted.begin(), sorted.end(), hi);` and return `last - first`.

require.message: Use `std::lower_bound` and `std::upper_bound` so each query is O(log n).

steps.title: Two pointers
steps.text:
On sorted data, two indexes moving toward each other often replace a nested loop. To find a pair summing to a target:

- start with `i` at the smallest and `j` at the largest,
- if the sum is too small, the only way to grow it is `i++`,
- if it's too big, `j--`.

Each step discards one element for good, so it's O(n) instead of O(n²).

**Your turn:** write `bool pair_sum(const std::vector<int>& sorted, long target)` that says whether two **different positions** hold values summing to `target`.
hints: Start `i = 0` and `j = size - 1`, and loop while `i < j`.
Add as long to avoid overflow; move i up when the sum is too small, j down when too big.

steps.title: Prefix sums
steps.text:
If you'll ask "what's the sum of elements l..r?" many times, precompute **prefix sums** once: `pre[i]` is the sum of the first i elements. Then any range sum is one subtraction:

```
sum(l..r) = pre[r + 1] - pre[l]
```

O(n) setup, then O(1) per query, instead of O(n) per query. The same trick works for counts, 2D grids ("summed-area tables") and time series.

**Your turn:** write class `RangeSum` with a constructor taking the values and `long long sum(int l, int r) const` for the inclusive range. The test runs 200,000 queries on 200,000 values.
hints: Store `std::vector<long long> pre_` with one more slot than the input, starting at 0.
`pre_[i + 1] = pre_[i] + v[i];` then `sum(l, r)` is `pre_[r + 1] - pre_[l]`.

steps.title: Challenge: sliding window
steps.text:
A **sliding window** keeps a range `[left, right]` that only ever moves forward. Each element enters once and leaves once, so the whole scan is O(n), even though it looks at many ranges.

**Your turn:** write `int longest_unique(const std::string& s)`: the length of the longest substring with **no repeated characters**. For `"abcabcbb"` it's 3 (`"abc"`).

Idea: move `right` forward one character at a time. If that character already appears inside the window, jump `left` past its previous position. Remember each character's last position in an array of 256 ints.
hints: Keep `std::array<int, 256> last` filled with -1: the last index where each byte was seen.
For each right: if `last[c] >= left`, move `left = last[c] + 1`. Then record `last[c] = right`.
The window length is `right - left + 1`; keep the maximum.

modules.title: Sorting algorithms
modules.summary: How sorting really works. Insertion sort, merge sort, quicksort partitioning, counting sort, stability with custom comparators, and quickselect.

steps.title: Insertion sort
steps.text:
**Insertion sort** grows a sorted prefix: take the next element and shift larger ones right until its spot opens up. Like sorting cards in your hand.

- O(n²) in general, but O(n) on data that's already *almost* sorted.
- Stable (equal elements keep their order) and in-place.
- Fastest of all for tiny arrays. Real `std::sort` implementations switch to it for ranges below about 16 elements.

```
for i in 1..n-1:
    key = v[i]; j = i - 1
    while j >= 0 and v[j] > key: v[j + 1] = v[j]; j--
    v[j + 1] = key
```

**Your turn:** implement `insertion_sort` and return how many element **shifts** it performed (a measure of how unsorted the input was).
hints: Loop i from 1; save `key = v[i]` and slide j down while `v[j - 1] > key`.
Using `j > 0` with `v[j - 1]` avoids a negative size_t index.
Count one shift each time you copy `v[j] = v[j - 1]`.

forbid.message: Implement the algorithm yourself on this step.

steps.title: Merge sort
steps.text:
**Merge sort** splits the array in half, sorts each half recursively, then **merges** the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front element.

- Always O(n log n), even in the worst case.
- Stable, which is why `std::stable_sort` is usually a merge sort.
- Needs O(n) extra memory for merging.

The merge step is the heart of it (you wrote one for strings in the STL module). **Your turn:** implement `merge_sort(std::vector<int>& v)`. The test sorts 200,000 numbers, so an O(n²) sort won't finish in time.
hints: Write a recursive helper that sorts the half-open range `[lo, hi)` using one shared temporary buffer.
Base case: fewer than 2 elements. Otherwise sort `[lo, mid)` and `[mid, hi)`, then merge into tmp and copy back.
When merging, take from the right half only if it's strictly smaller; that keeps the sort stable.

forbid.message: Implement merge sort yourself on this step.

steps.title: Quicksort and partitioning
steps.text:
**Quicksort** picks a *pivot*, **partitions** the array so smaller elements come before it and larger after, then recursively sorts both sides. No merging needed.

- O(n log n) on average, in place, and very fast in practice.
- O(n²) worst case with bad pivots (for example, always the last element of already-sorted data). That's why real implementations pick pivots carefully and `std::sort` falls back to heapsort when recursion gets too deep ("introsort").

The **Lomuto** partition, using the last element as the pivot:

```
pivot = v[hi]; i = lo
for j in lo..hi-1:
    if v[j] < pivot: swap(v[i], v[j]); i++
swap(v[i], v[hi])     // pivot lands at its final position i
return i
```

**Your turn:** write `int partition(std::vector<int>& v, int lo, int hi)` (inclusive range) and `void quick_sort(std::vector<int>& v, int lo, int hi)`.
hints: partition: `int pivot = v[hi]; int i = lo;` then for each j < hi, swap smaller elements to position i.
Finally swap the pivot into place: `std::swap(v[i], v[hi]); return i;`
quick_sort: stop when `lo >= hi`, else partition and recurse on both sides of p.

forbid.message: Implement the partition yourself on this step.

steps.title: Counting sort
steps.text:
Comparison sorts can't beat O(n log n). But when the values are **small integers** in a known range `0..k`, you don't need comparisons at all: count how many times each value occurs, then write them back in order. That's O(n + k).

It's the core of radix sort, and it's why sorting a million ages or exam scores is basically instant.

**Your turn:** write `void counting_sort(std::vector<int>& v, int max_value)` for values in `0..max_value`.
hints: `std::vector<int> count(max_value + 1, 0);` and `count[x]++` for every x.
Then walk value from 0 to max_value, writing it `count[value]` times.

forbid.message: Count, don't compare, on this step.

steps.title: Stability and custom comparators
steps.text:
A sort is **stable** if equal elements keep their original relative order. It matters when sorting records by one key after another, or when the input order means something (like arrival time).

- `std::sort`: not stable, usually slightly faster
- `std::stable_sort`: stable

A comparator must be a **strict weak ordering**: return true only when a should come *strictly* before b. Using `<=` instead of `<` breaks this rule and is undefined behavior; with `std::sort` it can even crash.

**Your turn:** write `void rank(std::vector<Entry>& v)` that orders entries by score, highest first. Entries with equal scores must stay in their original (sign-up) order.
hints: Use `std::stable_sort` with a lambda comparator.
Highest first: `return a.score > b.score;`

forbid.message: A comparator must be strict: use `>` or `<`, never `<=` or `>=`.

steps.title: Challenge: quickselect
steps.text:
To find the k-th smallest element (a median, a percentile, "the 95th percentile latency"), you don't need to sort everything. **Quickselect** partitions like quicksort but only recurses into the side that contains position k, which gives **O(n) on average**. `std::nth_element` does exactly this.

**Your turn:** write `int kth_smallest(std::vector<int> v, int k)` (k is 0-based; the vector is passed by value so you may rearrange it) using your own partition loop. Pick the **middle** element as the pivot (swap it to the end first) so already-sorted input stays fast.
hints: Loop with a range `[lo, hi]`. Swap the middle element to hi and partition like Lomuto.
After partitioning, the pivot is at its final index i. If k == i you're done; otherwise narrow the range to the side containing k.
When lo == hi, that single element is the answer.

forbid.message: Write the partition loop yourself.

modules.title: Hash tables
modules.summary: Build the data structure behind unordered_map. Buckets and chaining, load factor and rehashing, a string-keyed map with erase, custom hashes for your own keys, and an LRU cache.

steps.title: Buckets and chaining
steps.text:
A **hash table** stores items in an array of *buckets*. A **hash function** turns a key into a number, and `hash % bucket_count` picks the bucket. Looking up a key only searches **one bucket**, so with a good hash and enough buckets, lookup is O(1) on average.

Two keys can land in the same bucket (a *collision*). **Separate chaining** handles that by making each bucket a small list:

```
bucket 0: [16] -> [48]
bucket 1: [ ]
bucket 2: [2] -> [34]
```

`std::hash<int>{}(key)` gives a hash for built-in types. For ints it's often just the value itself.

**Your turn:** write `IntSet` with 16 buckets (a `std::vector<std::list<int>>`): `bool insert(int)` (false if already present), `bool contains(int) const`, and `std::size_t size() const`.
hints: Write a helper: `std::size_t bucket_of(int key) const { return std::hash<int>{}(key) % buckets_.size(); }`
insert: search that bucket's list with `std::find`; if absent, push_back and grow size_.
contains: same search, return whether it was found.

forbid.message: Build it from buckets yourself on this step.

steps.title: Load factor and rehashing
steps.text:
With a fixed 16 buckets, a million keys means about 62,500 per bucket, and "O(1)" becomes a slow linear search. The **load factor** is `size / bucket_count`. When it passes a threshold (0.75 is common; `std::unordered_map` uses 1.0), the table **rehashes**: it allocates about twice as many buckets and reinserts every key, because each key's bucket depends on the bucket count.

Rehashing is O(n), but it happens so rarely (each time the size doubles) that insertion stays **O(1) amortized**, the same argument as `std::vector` growth.

**Your turn:** extend `IntSet` so that after an insert makes `size > 0.75 * bucket_count`, it rehashes into twice as many buckets. The test inserts 200,000 keys, which is only fast if the table grows.
hints: After a successful insert, check `size_ * 4 > buckets_.size() * 3` (0.75 without floating point).
rehash: swap the buckets into a local `old`, give buckets_ twice as many empty lists, then re-insert every key from old.
Swapping first means bucket_of() already uses the new bucket count while re-inserting.

forbid.message: Grow your own table on this step.

steps.title: A string-keyed map with erase
steps.text:
A map stores **key/value pairs** in the buckets instead of bare keys. Erasing finds the pair in its bucket and removes it from the list.

`std::hash<std::string>` hashes strings. (Under the hood it runs something like the FNV or MurmurHash functions over the bytes.)

**Your turn:** write `StrMap` (a fixed 64 buckets is fine here) with:

- `void put(const std::string& key, int value)`: insert or overwrite
- `const int* get(const std::string& key) const`: pointer to the value, or `nullptr`
- `bool erase(const std::string& key)`
- `std::size_t size() const`
hints: Each bucket is a list of `std::pair<std::string, int>`. Find the bucket with `std::hash<std::string>{}(key) % buckets_.size()`.
put: if the key is in the bucket, overwrite `.second`; otherwise `emplace_back(key, value)`.
get returns `&kv.second` for a match. erase walks with an iterator and calls `b.erase(it)`.

forbid.message: Build the map from your own buckets on this step.

steps.title: Hashing your own keys
hints: PointHash combines the two int hashes with the formula shown above.
`std::unordered_set<Point, PointHash> seen{{0, 0}};` starts with the origin.
After each move, `if (!seen.insert(p).second) count++;`

steps.title: Challenge: an LRU cache
steps.text:
A **least-recently-used cache** keeps the `capacity` most recently used items and evicts the stalest one when full. It sits in front of databases, file systems and web servers everywhere, and it's one of the most common interview questions because it combines two structures:

- a `std::list` of `(key, value)` pairs ordered by recency (front = most recent),
- a `std::unordered_map` from key to the **list iterator**, for O(1) lookup.

`list.splice(list.begin(), list, it)` moves an element to the front in O(1) **without invalidating** any iterators, so the map stays correct.

**Your turn:** write `LruCache` with `std::optional<int> get(int key)` (a hit makes the key most recent) and `void put(int key, int value)` (insert or update, making it most recent; evict the least recent if over capacity). Both O(1).
hints: get: find the key in where_; if found, `items_.splice(items_.begin(), items_, it->second)` and return the value.
put on an existing key: update the value and splice it to the front.
put on a new key: `emplace_front`, record `where_[key] = items_.begin()`, and if over capacity erase `items_.back()` from both structures.

modules.title: Trees and heaps
modules.summary: Recursive thinking with trees. Binary tree basics, binary search trees, traversals and validation, level-order with a queue, a binary heap by hand, and a trie for autocomplete.

steps.title: Binary trees and recursion
hints: Base case: `if (!n) return 0;`
height is 1 + the larger of the two subtree heights; sum is the value plus both subtree sums.
Use `.get()` to pass a child's raw pointer without giving up ownership.

steps.title: Binary search trees
hints: Walk a pointer-to-slot down from `&root_`; stop at an empty slot.
Go left when `key < (*slot)->key`, right when greater, and return false on equality.
contains is the same walk with a plain `const Node*`.

steps.title: Traversals and validation
steps.text:
Three classic depth-first orders visit every node:

- **pre-order**: node, left, right (copying a tree, serializing it)
- **in-order**: left, node, right (a BST comes out **sorted**)
- **post-order**: left, right, node (deleting a tree, evaluating an expression tree)

In-order gives a neat BST check, but there's a subtler direct one: every node must lie within a **range** inherited from its ancestors. Checking only that each child is on the correct side of its parent is a classic wrong answer: a node can be right of its parent but still too big for its grandparent.

**Your turn:** write `void in_order(const Node* n, std::vector<int>& out)` and `bool is_bst(const Node* n, long lo, long hi)` that checks all keys lie strictly between lo and hi (the test calls it with `LONG_MIN`, `LONG_MAX`).
hints: in_order: recurse left, push the key, recurse right.
is_bst: an empty subtree is fine. Otherwise the key must satisfy lo < key < hi.
Going left tightens the upper bound to the key; going right tightens the lower bound.

steps.title: Level order with a queue
hints: Use `std::queue<const Node*>` starting with the root.
Each round, read `q.size()` first, then pop exactly that many nodes into one level vector, pushing their children.

steps.title: A binary heap by hand
steps.text:
A **binary heap** is a complete binary tree stored in a plain array. No pointers at all:

```
index:    0   1   2   3   4   5
parent(i) = (i - 1) / 2      children(i) = 2i + 1, 2i + 2
```

In a **min-heap**, every parent is ≤ its children, so the minimum is always at index 0.

- **push**: append at the end, then *sift up*: swap with the parent while smaller.
- **pop**: move the last element to the root, then *sift down*: swap with the smaller child while larger.

Both are O(log n). This is what's inside `std::priority_queue`.

**Your turn:** implement `MinHeap::push`, `MinHeap::pop` (assume non-empty) and `top`.
hints: push: append, then while i > 0 and the parent `(i - 1) / 2` is bigger, swap and move up.
pop: move the last element to index 0, pop_back, then sift down.
Sift down: find the smallest of i, 2i+1 and 2i+2 (those that exist); stop if it's i, else swap and continue.

forbid.message: Implement the sift-up and sift-down loops yourself on this step.

steps.title: Challenge: a trie for autocomplete
steps.text:
A **trie** (prefix tree) stores strings character by character: each node has up to 26 children, one per letter, and a flag marking where a word ends. Every word sharing a prefix shares that path, so "how many words start with `de_`?" takes O(length of the prefix), no matter how many words there are. Search boxes, spell checkers and routers use tries.

**Your turn:** write class `Trie` for lowercase words:

- `void insert(const std::string& w)`
- `bool contains(const std::string& w) const`: exact word
- `int count_prefix(const std::string& p) const`: how many inserted words start with p (store a counter in every node you pass during insert)
- `std::vector<std::string> complete(const std::string& p, std::size_t limit) const`: up to `limit` words with that prefix, in alphabetical order (a depth-first walk visiting children 'a' to 'z' produces them sorted)

Inserting the same word twice counts it once.
hints: insert: skip if already contained. Walk from the root creating missing children, incrementing `pass` on every node (including the root).
Write a private `find(prefix)` that returns the node at the end of the prefix, or nullptr.
complete: from that node, depth-first over children 0..25, appending letters to a running string and collecting words where `end` is true, until you have `limit`.

modules.title: Graphs
modules.summary: Model connections. Adjacency lists, breadth-first shortest paths on a grid, depth-first flood fill, topological sort for build order, Dijkstra with a priority queue, and union-find.

steps.title: Adjacency lists
steps.text:
A **graph** is a set of *vertices* (numbered 0..n-1 here) connected by *edges*. Road maps, social networks, build dependencies and network topologies are all graphs.

The standard representation is an **adjacency list**: for each vertex, the list of its neighbors.

```cpp
std::vector<std::vector<int>> adj(n);
adj[a].push_back(b);     // edge a -> b
adj[b].push_back(a);     // ...and b -> a if the graph is undirected
```

It uses O(V + E) memory, far less than an n × n matrix for the sparse graphs you meet in practice.

**Your turn:** write `build(n, edges, directed)` returning the adjacency list, and `int max_degree(const std::vector<std::vector<int>>& adj)` returning the largest number of neighbors any vertex has.
hints: `Graph adj(n);` then for each edge `adj[a].push_back(b);` and, if undirected, the reverse.
max_degree is the largest `adj[v].size()`.

steps.title: Shortest path with BFS
steps.text:
When every edge has the same cost, **breadth-first search** finds shortest paths: it explores everything 1 step away, then 2 steps, and so on, so the first time it reaches a cell is by a shortest route.

Grids are graphs too: each open cell is a vertex connected to its up/down/left/right neighbors.

```
dist[start] = 0; queue = [start]
while queue not empty:
    cur = pop front
    for each open neighbor nb with no dist yet:
        dist[nb] = dist[cur] + 1; push nb
```

**Your turn:** write `int shortest_path(const std::vector<std::string>& grid)` returning the fewest moves from `S` to `E`, moving through `.` cells (not `#`), or -1 if E can't be reached.
hints: Keep `dist` as a grid of -1 (unvisited). Find S, set its distance to 0 and push it.
Pop the front; if it's E return its distance. Otherwise push each in-bounds, non-wall, unvisited neighbor with distance + 1.
If the queue empties first, return -1.

steps.title: Depth-first flood fill
steps.text:
**Depth-first search** follows one path as far as it can before backtracking. It's the natural tool for "which things are connected?": pick an unvisited vertex, DFS from it to mark its whole component, and count how many times you had to start.

Recursive DFS is elegant, but a big component can overflow the call stack (the default stack is only about 1 MB, and on this site even less). Production code often uses an **explicit stack** instead:

```cpp
std::vector<std::pair<int, int>> stack = {{r, c}};
while (!stack.empty()) { auto [r, c] = stack.back(); stack.pop_back(); ... push neighbors ... }
```

**Your turn:** write `int count_islands(std::vector<std::string> grid)`, counting groups of `#` cells connected up/down/left/right. Use an explicit stack: the test has an island of 250,000 cells.
hints: Scan every cell. When you find a `#`, count a new island and flood it.
Flood with a vector used as a stack: mark cells as visited (turn them into '.') when you push them, so none is pushed twice.
Taking the grid by value lets you modify your own copy.

steps.title: Topological sort
steps.text:
Build systems, package managers, spreadsheets and job schedulers must run tasks **after** their dependencies. For a directed graph with no cycles, a **topological order** lists every vertex before everything that depends on it.

**Kahn's algorithm**:

1. Count each vertex's *in-degree* (how many edges point to it).
2. Put every vertex with in-degree 0 in a queue: nothing blocks it.
3. Pop one, append it to the order, and decrement the in-degree of its dependents; any that reach 0 join the queue.

If the order ends up shorter than n, some vertices were never freed: the graph has a **cycle** (for example, two libraries that depend on each other).

**Your turn:** write `std::vector<int> build_order(int n, const std::vector<std::pair<int, int>>& deps)` where `{a, b}` means "a must be built before b". Use a **min-heap** instead of a plain queue so ties come out smallest-number first (the tests expect that exact order). Return an empty vector if there's a cycle.
hints: Build an adjacency list and an in-degree count from the dependency pairs.
Seed a `std::priority_queue<int, std::vector<int>, std::greater<int>>` with all in-degree-0 vertices.
Pop, append, decrement dependents, push any that hit 0. Return {} if the order is shorter than n.

steps.title: Dijkstra's shortest paths
hints: Build an adjacency list of (neighbor, cost) pairs.
Use a min-heap of (distance, vertex): `std::priority_queue<Item, std::vector<Item>, std::greater<Item>>`.
Skip popped entries whose distance is larger than the best known one; relax each edge and push improvements.

steps.title: Challenge: union-find
steps.text:
**Union-find** (disjoint set union) tracks which items are in the same group while groups keep merging: network connectivity, clustering, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, detecting cycles as edges arrive.

Each set is a tree; `find(x)` walks to the root, which identifies the set. Two tricks make it nearly O(1) per operation:

- **path compression**: while finding, point nodes directly at the root
- **union by size**: attach the smaller tree under the larger one

**Your turn:** write class `UnionFind`:

- `explicit UnionFind(int n)`: n separate sets
- `int find(int x)` with path compression
- `bool unite(int a, int b)`: merge; returns false if already in the same set
- `int groups() const`: number of separate sets
- `int size_of(int x)`: size of x's set
hints: Store `parent_` (initialized to 0..n-1 with std::iota), `size_` (all 1) and a group counter.
find: walk up to the root, then walk again pointing every node on the path straight at the root.
unite: find both roots; if equal return false. Attach the smaller root under the larger, add sizes, decrement groups.

modules.title: Capstone: code review
modules.summary: Review realistic pull requests the way a senior engineer would. Each step hides several real bugs (off-by-one errors, dangling references, leaks on error paths, invalidated iterators, integer overflow and broken class design) for you to find and fix.

steps.title: Review: pagination
steps.text:
Reading other people's code critically is half of a professional developer's job. In a code review, ask of every line: **what inputs break this?** Empty input, the first and last item, zero, negative numbers, huge numbers.

A teammate opened this pull request for the leaderboard API. The spec says:

- `page` is **1-based** (page 1 is the first page)
- pages past the end return an empty list, never crash
- `page < 1` or `per_page < 1` returns an empty list

The tests here are the reviewer's edge cases. **Your turn:** find and fix the bugs. There are three.
